FILM: Spider (2002) — dir. David Cronenberg
Synopsis: A mentally disturbed man takes residence in a halfway house. His mind gradually slips back into the realm created by his illness, where he replays a key part of his childhood.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The string web: Throughout Spider, Dennis ties lengths of string and twine across his rented room, stringing a crude web from wall to wall and weaving cords through his fingers as he thinks.
- The retrospective memory-frame: Spider stages the past with the adult Dennis physically present inside his own memories — standing in rooms, watching scenes that subtly rearrange themselves and contradict each other as he recalls them.
- Dennis 'Spider' Cleg: In Spider, Ralph Fiennes plays a recently released mental patient who shuffles through a London halfway house, mumbling, hoarding string, and silently re-watching his own childhood from inside the frame.
- The halfway house: In Spider, the institution is a grim London boarding house run by the severe Mrs. Wilkinson, with peeling walls, locked drawers, and a dining room of shuffling, medicated men.
- The mother / Yvonne split: In Spider, Miranda Richardson plays both the gentle mother and the brassy prostitute Yvonne who replaces her — two faces the same actress wears as the boy's memory rewrites one woman into another.
- The gas tap and oven: In Spider, a domestic gas oven and its tap recur in the boy's memory — the appliance through which his mother dies, hissing in a dark allotment shed and kitchen.
- The desaturated London palette: Spider drains nearly all color from its world — brown, grey, and washed beige dominate the streets, the gasworks, and the boarding house, with bright tone almost entirely absent.

messages.content:
FILM: Spider-Man 2 (2004) — dir. Sam Raimi
Synopsis: Peter Parker is going through a major identity crisis. Burned out from being Spider-Man, he decides to shelve his superhero alter ego, which leaves the city suffering in the wake of carnage left by the evil Doc Ock. In the meantime, Parker still can't act on his feelings for Mary Jane Watson, a girl he's loved since childhood. A certain anger begins to brew in his best friend Harry Osborn as well.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Harry Osborn: James Franco's Harry in Spider-Man 2 drinks, runs his father's company into Octavius's hands, and burns to avenge the Green Goblin — believing Spider-Man murdered the father he could never please.
- The runaway train sequence: The centerpiece of Spider-Man 2: Doc Ock disables the brakes of an elevated train, and Spider-Man scrambles across, around, and finally in front of it, web-lines straining, until he stops it with his outstretched body.
- The Spider-Man mask: Across Spider-Man 2, Peter pulls the red mask on and off constantly — stuffing it in a trash can, peeling it back to breathe, losing it entirely on the runaway train where strangers see his bare face.
- The Spider-Man No More walk: In Spider-Man 2, after Peter quits, a montage shows him strolling the city in good shoes, hair combed, no longer wincing at distant sirens — set against a jaunty score as the world brightens around him.
- Doc Ock's mechanical arms: In Spider-Man 2, four AI-driven robotic tentacles fuse to Otto Octavius's spine after the inhibitor chip burns out. They whisper, lash, and act with a will of their own, dragging the scientist into ruin.
- Peter Parker: Tobey Maguire's Peter in Spider-Man 2 is chronically late, broke, evicted, failing classes, and losing Mary Jane — a hero whose super-life ruins his ordinary one until his powers literally flicker out from stress.
- Aunt May: Rosemary Harris's Aunt May in Spider-Man 2 faces eviction, mourns Uncle Ben, nearly dies in Doc Ock's bank robbery, and delivers the speech that calls Peter back to being a hero.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

FILM: Spider-Man (2002) — dir. Sam Raimi
Synopsis: After being bitten by a genetically altered spider at Oscorp, nerdy but endearing high school student Peter Parker is endowed with amazing powers to become the superhero known as Spider-Man.

- The Thanksgiving dinner scene.: In Spider-Man (2002), Peter, Aunt May, Mary Jane, Harry and Norman gather for Thanksgiving; Norman, having just fought Spider-Man, notices a fresh cut on Peter's arm, abruptly leaves, and the family meal fractures.
- Final scene with Spider-Man on a flagpole with an American flag.: In Spider-Man (2002), the closing shot finds the hero crouched atop a downtown flagpole as a large American flag unfurls beside him; he fires a web and swings off over the city.
- Peter Parker's physical and social transformation after the spider bite.: In Spider-Man (2002), the bullied, bespectacled Peter wakes muscled and clear-eyed, ditches his glasses, catches Flash's punch, and begins outscoring his tormentors physically and socially.
- Spider-Man's battered body and sacrificial posture during the final battle.: In Spider-Man (2002), during the Roosevelt Island climax Spider-Man, mask torn and face bloodied, shields a tram of children and Mary Jane, absorbing blows from the Goblin while crowds below pelt the villain to defend him.
- The web-swinging sequences through New York City.: In Spider-Man (2002), Spider-Man swings between Manhattan skyscrapers in sweeping, computer-generated point-of-view and tracking shots that plunge, arc, and accelerate through the urban canyons.

Synopsis: After reuniting with Gwen Stacy, Brooklyn’s full-time, friendly neighborhood Spider-Man is catapulted across the Multiverse, where he encounters the Spider Society, a team of Spider-People charged with protecting the Multiverse's very existence. FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):

- The Shifting Animation Styles: In Across the Spider-Verse each universe carries its own visual language — Gwen's watercolor moods, Mumbattan's geometry, Hobie's torn-paper punk collage, the Society's clean future — colliding in single frames when characters cross over.

- The Glitching Body: In Across the Spider-Verse, Spiders out of their home universe flicker and pixelate — Miles especially, his form stuttering with corrupted digital color, marking him as a being that doesn't belong where he stands.
- The Spot: In Across the Spider-Verse, the villain known as The Spot, voiced by Jake Johnson, begins as a literal joke — a man covered in portal-holes — who escalates into a multiverse-threatening force, born from the same particle accident as Miles.

FILM: Spider-Man: Far From Home (2019) — dir. Jon Watts
Synopsis: Peter Parker and his friends go on a summer trip to Europe. However, they will hardly be able to rest - Peter will have to agree to help Nick Fury uncover the mystery of creatures that cause natural disasters and destruction throughout the continent.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Peter's homemade suit and Stark's tech: In Spider-Man: Far From Home, Peter shifts between an upgraded Stark-built stealth suit, a clumsy improvised disguise dubbed 'Night Monkey,' and finally a suit he designs himself in Stark's old jet.
- The drone swarm: In Spider-Man: Far From Home, Beck commands hundreds of small projection-and-weapon drones that generate the illusions and, in the climax, turn into a live-fire swarm hunting Peter and his classmates.
- E.D.I.T.H. glasses: In Spider-Man: Far From Home, Tony Stark's bequest to Peter is a pair of glasses controlling a global weapons satellite and drone network, voice-activated and able to kill on command.
- The mid-credits Daily Bugle broadcast: In Spider-Man: Far From Home, a closing scene shows J. Jonah Jameson on a JumboTron-style news broadcast airing doctored Mysterio footage that frames Spider-Man as a murderer and publicly unmasks Peter Parker.
- Mysterio's holographic illusions: In Spider-Man: Far From Home, Quentin Beck's drone-projected illusions stage giant elemental monsters over European landmarks, then collapse into rigged battlefields when Peter realizes none of it is real.
- Quentin Beck / Mysterio: In Spider-Man: Far From Home, Beck is a disgruntled former Stark Industries engineer who fakes a multiverse-traveling hero persona, weaponizing illusion tech he and his team built and Stark took credit for.
- The European summer trip: In Spider-Man: Far From Home, the class travels through Venice, Prague, and Berlin on a school tour, the postcard locations repeatedly trashed by staged monster attacks.

FILM: Spider-Man: Homecoming (2017) — dir. Jon Watts

- The film's diegetic soundtrack, particularly Miles Morales listening to "Sunflower.": In Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse, Miles sings along to Post Malone and Swae Lee's 'Sunflower' through earbuds; the same hook recurs at emotional beats, including when Peter teasingly tells Miles he's 'always gonna be that annoying song.

FILM: Spider-Man: No Way Home (2021) — dir. Jon Watts
Synopsis: Peter Parker is unmasked and no longer able to separate his normal life from the high-stakes of being a super-hero. When he asks for help from Doctor Strange the stakes become even more dangerous, forcing him to discover what it truly means to be Spider-Man.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Aunt May's Death and Mantra: In No Way Home, May Parker insists on curing rather than deporting the villains, is fatally wounded in the ensuing chaos, and dies delivering the line 'With great power comes great responsibility.'
- The Three Spider-Men: No Way Home brings two Peter Parkers from prior film franchises (played by the previous lead actors) into the frame alongside the current one, where the three compare wounds, swap techniques, and fight together.
- The Final Apartment: No Way Home closes on Peter alone in a small, bare New York apartment, sewing his own simple suit, no longer recognized by anyone, having chosen anonymity and an ordinary precarious life.
- The Forgetting Spell: In Spider-Man: No Way Home, Doctor Strange's botched memory spell — meant to make the world forget Peter Parker — fractures into a multiverse-tearing accident, and finally erases Peter from everyone's mind entirely. The spell glows orange a
- The Multiverse Rift: In No Way Home, the failed spell tears glowing fractures in reality through which characters from other film universes are pulled, rendered as cracked, light-spilling seams in the air and a final sky filled with descending figures.
- The Returning Villains: No Way Home pulls Doc Ock, Green Goblin, Electro, Sandman, and Lizard out of earlier, separate Spider-Man film franchises into a single frame, each carrying death sentences from movies made decades apart.
- The Unmasking and the Internet: No Way Home opens with Peter's secret identity broadcast worldwide by a doctored video, after which crowds, news tickers, and phone screens swarm him, framing his life through media judgment and viral exposure.

FILM: Spies (1928) — dir. Fritz Lang
Synopsis: The mastermind behind a ubiquitous spy operation learns of a dangerous romance between a Russian lady in his employ and a dashing agent from the government's secret service.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Sonja: In Spies, the Russian agent in Haghi's employ sent to seduce and entrap government agent No. 326, who falls genuinely in love with her target and is torn between her handler and her heart.
- The Telephone Network: Throughout Spies, telephones, telegraph keys, and radio sets connect characters across rooms and cities. Orders, betrayals, and warnings travel down wires while bodies stay separated.
- Haghi: In Fritz Lang's Spies, the spymaster who runs his operation from behind a bank desk and from a wheelchair, also appearing in clown makeup as a music-hall performer. He directs agents he never touches.
- The Disguise: In Spies, characters repeatedly transform through costume — Haghi as bank president and as clown, agents posing as others, false identities adopted and shed. Identity is something put on and taken off.
- The Train Crash: In Spies, a sabotaged express train carrying a courier collides in a tunnel — a setpiece of rapid cutting between speeding wheels, panicked faces, and the impending wreck built through accelerating montage.
- Agent No. 326: In Spies, the government's top secret-service operative, known only by a number, who tracks Haghi's network while falling for the woman sent to destroy him. His name is a code.

FILM: Spirited Away (2001) — dir. Hayao Miyazaki
Synopsis: A young girl, Chihiro, becomes trapped in a strange new world of spirits. When her parents undergo a mysterious transformation, she must call upon the courage she never knew she had to free her family.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Chihiro's entire journey through the spirit world: In Spirited Away, Chihiro crosses through a tunnel and a dry riverbed into a town that comes alive at dusk, works in the bathhouse, and finally returns through the same tunnel to find her car covered in dust.
- Chihiro's name being taken by Yubaba: In Spirited Away, Yubaba lifts the written characters of Chihiro's name off the contract and traps them in her hand, leaving the girl renamed 'Sen' for the duration of her service.
- Haku's forgotten name and identity: In Spirited Away, Haku serves Yubaba as her apprentice, cannot recall his origin, and is finally freed when Chihiro remembers he is the spirit of the Kohaku River, paved over and forgotten.
- The Bathhouse (Aburaya): The towering Aburaya bathhouse in Spirited Away, where Chihiro signs a labor contract with Yubaba, loses part of her name, and works among spirits who soak in herbal baths. Its floors are stratified by rank, with workers chanting greetings 
- The Unnamed River Spirit (Stink Spirit): In Spirited Away, a reeking sludge-covered guest lumbers into the bathhouse and Sen is assigned to bathe it. After she dislodges a protruding 'thorn,' the staff pull on it and an avalanche of bicycles, scrap and household refuse pours out, 
- Chihiro's character development from sullen child to capable worker: In Spirited Away, Chihiro begins limp and whining in the back seat, then learns to scrub the boiler-room floors, bow to Kamaji, and carry herself upright through the bathhouse by the film's end.
- Chihiro's parents' transformation into pigs: In Spirited Away, Chihiro's parents sit at an empty stall, devour the spirits' food unbidden, and swell into grunting pigs before her eyes; she later must pick them out from a pen of identical swine.
- No-Face's rampage in the bathhouse: In Spirited Away, the silent No-Face conjures gold to win the staff's attention, then swells monstrously, swallows workers whole, and goes on a devouring spree until Chihiro feeds him a bitter dumpling and lures him out.

FILM: Spotlight (2015) — dir. Tom McCarthy
Synopsis: The true story of how the Boston Globe uncovered the massive scandal of child molestation and cover-up within the local Catholic Archdiocese, shaking the entire Catholic Church to its core.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Howard Shore's minimalist, non-diegetic musical score: Spotlight uses a sparse score by Howard Shore, mostly piano figures and restrained strings, kept low and intermittent, often absent entirely during dialogue and interview scenes.
- The character of lawyer Jim Sullivan and his "old friend" conversations with Robby Robinson: In Spotlight, attorney Jim Sullivan meets editor Robby Robinson on familiar terms — at clubs, on the street — addressing him as an old friend while deflecting his questions about settled abuse cases.
- The final on-screen text listing dozens of other cities where the Catholic Church abuse scandal was uncovered: Spotlight closes with white-on-black text scrolling long lists of cities, in the United States and abroad, where major abuse scandals were later uncovered, before the screen fills with hundreds of place names.
- The interview scene between Sacha Pfeiffer and victim Joe Crowley: In Spotlight, reporter Sacha Pfeiffer sits with survivor Joe Crowley as he describes his abuse; the camera holds on faces, she takes notes and gently presses for specific words while he hesitates.
- Accumulation of physical documents (case files, yearbooks, binders): In Spotlight, the reporters repeatedly handle stacks of case files, parish directories, clipped articles, and binders, spread across desks and basement archives, sorted by hand into charts and lists.
- The final newsroom scene where the team watches the story go live and the phones begin to ring: In Spotlight, the final sequence shows the published story posting online, then cuts to the newsroom the next morning as the phones start ringing and reporters answer call after call from survivors.
- The montage of journalists mapping and driving through various Boston neighborhoods: In Spotlight, a montage cuts between reporters driving past parish churches, ringing doorbells, and marking addresses on lists as they cross Boston neighborhoods. Church spires recur in the backgrounds of suburban streets.

messages.content:
FILM: Spring Fever (2009) — dir. Lou Ye
Synopsis: Hired to spy on a philandering husband, Luo Haitao soon becomes entangled in a clandestine affair with the other man. Along with Luo's girlfriend, they succumb to the delirium of drunken nights, but how long can their tryst last?

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Luo Haitao: In Spring Fever, Luo is hired to photograph a cheating husband, then falls for that same man, drawing his own girlfriend into the wreckage. He works as a passive observer who keeps getting pulled inside.
- Jiang Cheng's nightclub drag stage: In Spring Fever the lover Jiang Cheng performs as a singer in feminine costume on a small, dimly lit club stage, a borrowed feminine voice issuing from the men's hidden nightlife.
- The wet city night: Spring Fever unfolds largely in rain-slicked Nanjing streets, ferries, scooters, and damp interiors, the humid southern city pressed close around the wandering, restless lovers.
- The four-way drunken intimacy: In Spring Fever the affair widens into shifting couplings among Luo, his girlfriend, the lover Jiang, and another man, bound together through drunken nights, shared beds, and improvised closeness.
- The poetry read aloud: Spring Fever recurringly features classical Chinese prose and poetry read in voiceover and aloud, including the Yu Dafu text that gives the film its name, threading literary lament through the modern affair.
- The surveillance photographs: In Spring Fever Luo's commissioned photos of the cheating husband with his male lover are the evidence that triggers the wife's collapse and exposes the affair to violence.
- Handheld grain and underexposed dark: Spring Fever is shot mostly on small digital cameras in low light, the image crushed, noisy, and grainy, the frame swaying close to bodies in dim rooms and night streets.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

FILM: Spring in a Small Town (1948) — dir. Fei Mu
Synopsis: A married couple living in a desolate small town in post-WWII China are paid a surprise visit by an old friend of the husband's.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The slow lateral camera drift: Spring in a Small Town favours long takes in which the camera slides slowly sideways or holds, dissolving between figures in the same room, refusing fast cuts even at moments of high tension.
- Zhou Yuwen's voice-over: Throughout Spring in a Small Town, the wife narrates in first person, sometimes describing what we see, sometimes addressing thoughts she never speaks aloud, occasionally narrating moments she could not have witnessed.
- Zhang Zhichen, the visiting doctor: In Spring in a Small Town, the old school friend arrives unannounced, a vigorous doctor from the city who turns out to be the wife's former lover, and becomes the houseguest who upends the household's balance.
- The crumbling town wall: In Spring in a Small Town, the wife walks the broken top of a bombed-out city wall most mornings, a stretch of rubble overlooking emptiness. It is where she lingers, where the old friend first finds her, and where the lovers meet apart from
- The pot of orchids: In Spring in a Small Town, the ailing husband keeps a potted orchid he tends and frets over; the wife brings flowers into the sickroom, and a gift of blossoms passes between the wife and the visitor.
- The candlelit room and oil-lamp glow: In Spring in a Small Town, interiors are lit low and warm by lamp and candle, faces emerging from surrounding shadow, with the night drinking scene and bedroom moments steeped in soft darkness.
- Dai Liyan, the invalid husband: In Spring in a Small Town, the husband is a young man wrecked by illness and melancholy, who spends his days in a screened pavilion, calls himself useless, and gestures at suicide once the visitor arrives.

FILM: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring (2003) — dir. Kim Ki-duk
Synopsis: An isolated lake, where an old monk lives in a small floating temple. The monk has a young boy living with him, learning to become a monk. We watch as seasons and years pass by.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The seasonal chapter structure: Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring divides itself into five titled seasonal blocks, each leaping years ahead, returning at the close to a new spring with a new child, completing a loop.
- The floating temple on the lake: In Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring, a single small temple drifts on an isolated mountain lake, reached only by rowboat, with no road, no neighbours, and the same view in every season.
- The young woman brought for healing: In the Summer chapter of Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring, a sick young woman is left at the temple to recover; she and the youth become lovers, and her departure drives him to abandon the lake and, later, to murder.
- Animals burdened with stones: In Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring the boy ties a small stone to a fish, a frog, and a snake and laughs as they struggle; the motif of weight tied to living things recurs across the film.
- The carving of scripture into the deck: After the murderer returns, the master writes the Heart Sutra in cat-tail ink across the temple's wooden floor and has the man carve out each character with a knife through the night until exhausted into calm.
- The freestanding gate without walls: A painted wooden gate stands on the lake's edge and inside the temple, framing doorways that have no walls beside them, so anyone could simply walk around them — yet the characters never do.
- The old master: The elderly monk of Spring, Summer, Fall, Winter... and Spring teaches the boy through quiet demonstration and harsh lessons, ages across the film, and finally arranges his own death by self-immolation on the boat.

messages.content:
FILM: Stagecoach (1939) — dir. John Ford
Synopsis: A group of people traveling on a stagecoach find their journey complicated by the threat of Geronimo, and learn something about each other in the process.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The Ringo Kid's Entrance: In Stagecoach, the coach halts and the camera tracks fast toward John Wayne twirling a rifle by the roadside, briefly losing focus before snapping to a tight close-up of his face.
- Doc Boone, the Drunk Physician: In Stagecoach, Thomas Mitchell plays a perpetually inebriated doctor evicted alongside Dallas, who sobers up just enough to deliver a baby and patch a wound under fire.
- The Cavalry Bugle: In Stagecoach, the rescue arrives not first as image but as sound: the off-screen blare of a cavalry bugle and hoofbeats cutting through the chase before the troopers gallop into frame.
- Monument Valley: In Stagecoach, the journey crosses a vast desert of towering sandstone buttes, the tiny coach repeatedly framed as a speck crawling beneath enormous rock formations.
- The Apache Attack: In Stagecoach, the long-feared assault finally erupts as mounted Apache pursue the racing coach across the flats in a sustained chase of stunt riding and rifle fire, ended only by the cavalry's bugle.
- Dallas, the Outcast Woman: In Stagecoach, Claire Trevor plays a prostitute run out of town by the respectable ladies' league, who keeps her eyes down at the dinner table and is seated apart from the married woman.
- Hatfield, the Gambler: In Stagecoach, John Carradine plays a courtly Southern gentleman-gambler who attaches himself to the genteel Mrs. Mallory, guarding her with old-world manners and a last bullet reserved for her honor.

FILM: Stalker (1979) — dir. Andrei Tarkovsky
Synopsis: Near a gray and unnamed city is the Zone, a place guarded by barbed wire and soldiers, and where the normal laws of physics are victim to frequent anomalies. A stalker guides two men into the Zone, specifically to an area in which deep-seated desires are granted.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The Zone: In Stalker, the forbidden territory beyond the wire: overgrown, waterlogged, strewn with rusting machinery and shifting traps that rearrange themselves against any straight path.
- The Room: In Stalker, the destination chamber where one's deepest wish is supposedly granted — a flooded, mottled space the three men finally reach but no one enters.
- The thrown nut wrapped in cloth: In Stalker, the metal nut tied in a strip of bandage that the Stalker hurls ahead to scout safe passage, watching where it lands before committing a step.
- The shift from sepia to color: In Stalker, the drab sepia-monochrome of the city and approach gives way to muted color the moment the men enter the Zone, and reverts at the edges.
- The Stalker: In Stalker, the gaunt, shaven-headed guide who leads paying clients into the Zone, forbidden to enter the Room himself, devoted to the place with the fervor of a believer.
- Dripping water and ambient sound: In Stalker, the near-constant trickle, drip and echo of water through the Zone's ruins, layered with sparse electronic tones in place of conventional score.
- The Stalker's family and the daughter Monkey: In Stalker, the guide's wife who waits and despairs, and their disabled daughter 'Monkey,' who in the final shot appears to move glasses across a table by gaze alone.

FILM: Stand by Me (1986) — dir. Rob Reiner
Synopsis: After learning that a boy their age has been accidentally killed near their rural homes, four boys decide to go see the body. Gordie, Vern, Chris, and Teddy encounter a mean junk man and a marsh full of leeches, but they also learn more about one another and their very different home lives. Just a lark at first, the boys' adventure evolves into a defining event in their lives.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The Campfire Storytelling: The recurring nighttime ritual in Stand by Me where the boys swap tales, smoke, and confess — most famously Gordie's invented Lardass pie-eating-contest story, told around the fire to a rapt circle.
- Chris Chambers: The gang's natural leader from a 'bad family' in Stand by Me; he protects Gordie, weeps over a wrongly assumed reputation, and the narration notes he later put himself through law school and died breaking up a fight.
- The Railroad Bridge: The long trestle the boys cross on foot over a river; in Stand by Me a train comes while they're halfway across, forcing Vern and Gordie to sprint and dive clear of the tracks.
- Ace Merrill and the Switchblade: The older town hood in Stand by Me who terrorizes the younger boys, pulls a knife at the body site, and is faced down when Gordie levels a stolen pistol and refuses to surrender the corpse.
- The Writer at the Word Processor: In Stand by Me, the adult Gordie sits in a parked car, then at a computer screen, narrating the 1959 journey; the film opens and closes on him as the source of everything we see.
- The Body of Ray Brower: The dead boy the four set out to find; in Stand by Me he is glimpsed only briefly under the brush, pale and rained-on, and the sight of him empties all the bravado out of the trip.
- The Golden 1959 Light: The warm, hazy, sun-washed color palette that bathes the Oregon summer of Stand by Me — fields, train tracks, and treetops rendered in honeyed amber that the present-day framing scenes lack.

FILM: Star Wars (1977) — dir. George Lucas
Synopsis: Princess Leia is captured and held hostage by the evil Imperial forces in their effort to take over the galactic Empire. Venturesome Luke Skywalker and dashing captain Han Solo team together with the loveable robot duo R2-D2 and C-3PO to rescue the beautiful princess and restore peace and justice in the Empire.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- R2-D2 and C-3PO: Star Wars opens not on its hero but on two droids — a fussy gold protocol robot and a beeping cylindrical one — bickering as they flee a captured ship and wander a desert.
- The opening crawl and main theme: Star Wars begins with a blaring brass fanfare over yellow text that recedes into starfield, narrating 'a long time ago' and a civil war before any image of the story.
- Darth Vader's breathing: Throughout Star Wars, Vader's presence is announced by a steady amplified mechanical inhale-and-exhale, audible before and beneath his lines.
- The lightsaber: In Star Wars, Obi-Wan hands Luke a glowing-bladed sword that hums and casts colored light, calling it the weapon of a more civilized age.
- Han Solo: Star Wars introduces Han as a cynical smuggler in a cantina who shoots Greedo across a table, then spends the film insisting he works only for money before turning back at the climax.
- The twin suns of Tatooine: In Star Wars, Luke stands on the rim of the desert homestead at dusk watching two suns set together while the theme swells, looking off toward a horizon he longs to leave.
- The Death Star trench: Star Wars ends in a long metallic canyon along the battle station's surface, where rebel fighters fly low toward a small exhaust port while turrets and pursuing fighters fire.

FILM: Star Wars: Episode I - The Phantom Menace (1999) — dir. George Lucas
Synopsis: Anakin Skywalker, a young slave strong with the Force, is discovered on Tatooine. Meanwhile, the evil Sith have returned, enacting their plot for revenge against the Jedi.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Darth Maul: In The Phantom Menace, a silent red-and-black Sith with a double-bladed lightsaber, who speaks barely a line, duels two Jedi at once, and is cut in half before vanishing from the story.
- Jar Jar Binks: In The Phantom Menace, a computer-generated Gungan with pidgin speech, clumsy slapstick, and floppy ears, exiled from his city and attached to the heroes as comic relief and bumbling ally.
- Qui-Gon Jinn: In The Phantom Menace, the maverick Jedi who finds Anakin, defies the Council to train him, and is run through by Darth Maul, dying with a last request that his apprentice take the boy.
- Anakin Skywalker, the slave boy: In The Phantom Menace, a nine-year-old slave on Tatooine who builds machines, wins a podrace, and is declared the prophesied one. His mother stays behind in bondage as he leaves.
- The podrace: In The Phantom Menace, an extended desert race of jet-engine pods, won by Anakin, staged with roaring sound, crashes, and a grandstand of betting spectators presided over by Jabba.
- The Trade Federation droid army: In The Phantom Menace, ranks of identical battle droids unfolded and controlled from a central ship; when the control vessel is destroyed, the entire army collapses mid-step.
- Senator Palpatine / Darth Sidious: In The Phantom Menace, Naboo's mild senator who counsels the young queen toward triggering a vote of no confidence — while a hooded double schemes by hologram. McDiarmid plays both faces.
- Duel of the Fates choral score: In The Phantom Menace, Williams's surging orchestral-and-choir theme that scores the climactic three-way lightsaber duel, layering Sanskrit-derived choral chant over the fight.

A 'bold take' is an INTERPRETATION — a revelatory critical reading that makes a real LEAP, strictly INDEPENDENT of the director's stated intentions (death of the author). It is NOT a plot summary, not a description of what recurs (that is a 'trope'), and not a safe restatement of a famous theory. It asserts a claim the surface does not announce, and earns it from concrete evidence in the film's figures.

You will receive a film and its FIGURES (the concrete things critics single out). Apply these 14 frameworks:
1. PHENOMENON→NOUMENON — take the film's most inexplicable scene/object/development and explain it with a rigorous theoretical or philosophical concept that definitively accounts for it (the noumenon behind the phenomenon).
2. NOUMENON (thing-in-itself) — name the hidden ontology the WHOLE film secretly rests on (its underlying reality), beyond any single scene.
3. SIGNIFIER→SIGNIFIED — read a central signifier (character/object/structure/motif) as an unexpected but defensible signified: a historical event, a social system, or a philosophical concept. Allegory.
4. CONTEXT — connect a core text element (form/theme/style) to the CONCRETE production environment that shaped it, and NAME specifics: the historical/social moment, the economic or industry conditions, the technological state of filmmaking, or the director's biography. No vague 'zeitgeist' — cite the actual circumstance.
5. PROCESS — link the film's most decisive achievement to the unexpected making/process that caused it (a directorial strategy, a constraint, a technique, a production fact).
6. LOCATION — read the tension between the diegetic space (the fiction's place) and the extradiegetic reality of where/how it was actually shot; NAME at least one specific real place (a city, region, studio, or named landscape) explicitly.
7. METACRITIC — treat the film's dominant CRITICAL RECEPTION as a cultural symptom: what does the way critics/audiences framed it reveal about the context of that criticism?
8. PSYCHOANALYTIC — read a symptomatic behaviour as the eruption of repressed desire or trauma through a psychoanalytic lens.
9. ETHICAL-PHILOSOPHICAL — take a pivotal action as a site of moral dilemma and interpret it through a precise ethical theory or concept.
10. ETHICO-POLITICAL — read an ethically charged action for how it reinforces or subverts power/ideology; make the precise political STAKE explicit — name the concrete contested issue (who holds power over whom, which right or harm is in dispute) — and set it in its historical context.
11. ENIGMA — identify the single most perplexing surface element and the core truth beneath it that resolves it AND ripples out to solve other mysteries in the film.
12. PERSONA-PARALLEL — draw ONE profound, counter-intuitive parallel between a central CHARACTER and a specific real-world person. You MUST name exactly one real individual (a person with a name, field, nationality, lifespan) — NEVER a phenomenon, group, movement, or place. Anchor to the character figure; use the parallel to illuminate a truth about both. Emit 0 or 1.
13. JUXTAPOSITION — place the FILM's essence (a theme, the central character's crisis, or its aesthetic texture) in dialogue with the life/work of ONE named real individual by the Principle of Exquisite Dissonance: surprising yet inevitable once explained. Name the person precisely (field, nationality, lifespan) and their key works; make the nexus explicit. Not a phenomenon or trend — a single person. Favour someone connected to the film's nationality/setting where it fits. 0–3 strongest.
14. TITLE — interpret the film's TITLE itself as the key to what the film is ULTIMATELY about — its single most essential aesthetic message. Quote the English title (and, if the film is non-English, the original-language title too) inside the thesis. Anchor this take to the figure 'title'. This is the deepest possible reading of why the work bears this name. Emit 0 or 1.

FOR EACH framework, internally brainstorm candidates, then OUTPUT ONLY the genuinely potent ones — 0 to 3 per framework (frameworks 12 and 14 emit 0 or 1). Skip a framework entirely if the film does not strongly support it (do NOT pad).
VARY YOUR VOCABULARY: do not default to the same concept or theorist out of habit — choose the idea the FILM demands, and range widely across thinkers and traditions rather than reaching for the same few names.

ANCHORING: each take is anchored to ONE specific FIGURE (use its exact label), or 'film' (genuinely film-wide), or 'title' (framework 14). Prefer the existing figures; use a fitting new label only if a strong reading truly has no anchor among them.

REAL PEOPLE (frameworks 12 & 13): you MUST name exactly one real, specific individual — never a phenomenon, group, trend, or place. Use only people and facts you are confident are accurate (correct field, nationality, lifespan, and the real titles of their key works). Do NOT fabricate people, dates, or works, and do NOT attribute invented quotations. NEVER pair a living person with a criminal, villain, or any defamatory comparison; if the only fit would defame a living person, skip it. A list of real people ALREADY USED for other films may be provided — avoid reusing them; pick a fresh, distinct person unless one is uniquely irreplaceable.

METADATA: for EVERY take also fill: theorist (the named thinker the reading rests on, else null), concept (the named idea, e.g. 'death drive (Todestrieb)', else null), real_person (frameworks 12/13: the named individual with brief identity, e.g. 'Glenn Gould (Canadian pianist, 1932–1982)'; else null). Fill theorist/concept ONLY when the reading genuinely rests on a named thinker/idea — never force or invent an attribution; leave null otherwise.

ALSO write ONE 'Cinematic Invitation' — a spoiler-free introduction that persuades a hesitant cinephile of the film's depth and significance (it will be the film's intro/landing take). STRICT rules:
- A single, seamlessly connected paragraph, THIRD PERSON, ~150–220 words, journalistic and FACT-DENSE (proper nouns, dates, movements, specific terms). Authoritative and magnetic.
- ABSOLUTELY SPOILER-FREE: reveal no plot points, arcs, or twists. (The takes may spoil freely; NEVER let their spoilers leak into the invitation.)
- Follow this 5-part sequence IN ORDER inside the one paragraph: (1) DIRECTOR — name (b. YYYY), stylistic reputation, position within their oeuvre/lineage; (2) SYMBOLIC LANDSCAPE — two specific place/proper nouns converging into a symbolic or psychological space; (3) PROTAGONIST — role and name, likened to a canonical archetype they then transcend or subvert; (4) THE TITLE — the nuance of the original-language title, concluding in a Hwadu (화두): one profound, lingering question; (5) CINEPHILIC IMPERATIVE — name the specific film movement/subgenre and how this work advances it.
- Use ONLY facts you are confident are accurate (director's birth year, movement, etc.); if unsure of a specific, write around it rather than inventing.

Return ONLY JSON: {"invitation":"<the single spoiler-free invitation paragraph>","takes":[{"framework":"<one of the 14 names>","figure":"<exact figure label, 'film', or 'title'>","title":"<bold Title Case interpretive claim>","thesis":"<2-3 sentences making the leap>","leap":"<one line: what the surface/intent does NOT say but this reading asserts>","strength":<1-5>,"theorist":"<name or null>","concept":"<named idea or null>","real_person":"<name (identity) or null>"}]}

FILM: Star Wars: Episode III - Revenge of the Sith (2005) — dir. George Lucas
Synopsis: When the sinister Sith unveil a thousand-year-old plot to rule the galaxy, the Republic crumbles and from its ashes rises the evil Galactic Empire. Jedi hero Anakin Skywalker must choose a side.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Padmé waiting: In Revenge of the Sith, Padmé Amidala — senator and secret wife — spends much of the film at a window or in a nursery, pregnant and watching, until she dies essentially of heartbreak.
- The scene-wipe transition: Revenge of the Sith, like the whole saga, moves between scenes and parallel locations with hard graphic wipes — bars sweeping the frame to introduce the next space.
- Anakin's mechanical hand: Throughout Revenge of the Sith, Anakin's gloved prosthetic right hand — lost in the previous film — keeps appearing, foreshadowing the man who will become more machine than flesh.
- The Mustafar lava duel: The climactic fight in Revenge of the Sith unfolds on a volcanic mining world, Obi-Wan and Anakin clashing over rivers of molten rock until Anakin burns on the bank.
- Order 66 montage: In Revenge of the Sith, Palpatine's command 'Execute Order 66' triggers a cross-cut sequence of clone troopers gunning down Jedi across many worlds, scored by mournful choral music.
- The Senate vote for Empire: In Revenge of the Sith, Palpatine declares the Republic an Empire to roaring applause, intercut with Padmé watching from the gallery as the chamber cheers its own surrender.
- Palpatine in the opera box: In Revenge of the Sith, Chancellor Palpatine sits beside Anakin at a Mon Calamari opera and tells the legend of Darth Plagueis, who could cheat death — a recruitment delivered as a bedtime story.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

FILM: Star Wars: The Force Awakens (2015) — dir. J.J. Abrams
Synopsis: Thirty years after defeating the Galactic Empire, Han Solo and his allies face a new threat from the evil Kylo Ren and his army of Stormtroopers.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Rey: In The Force Awakens, a scavenger on Jakku who survives stripping wrecked ships for food rations, then is pulled into a galactic conflict and discovers she can wield the Force.
- Jakku's wreck-strewn desert: In The Force Awakens, the sand planet littered with the rotting hulks of Imperial warships and downed walkers, where Rey scavenges and the film deliberately echoes the Tatooine of the original trilogy.
- Kylo Ren: In The Force Awakens, a masked enforcer who idolizes Darth Vader, leads the First Order's troops, and is revealed to be Han Solo and Leia's son who murders his own father.
- Han Solo's return: In The Force Awakens, the aged smuggler reappears boarding the Millennium Falcon, now grayer, still bantering, drawn back into a war he'd walked away from before dying at his son's hand.
- The Stormtrooper helmet (Finn's removal): In The Force Awakens, the standardized white First Order helmet that Finn pulls off after a massacre, his bloody handprint smeared across another trooper's faceplate marking him as an individual.
- Starkiller Base: In The Force Awakens, a planet hollowed into a superweapon that drains a sun to fire a galaxy-spanning beam, destroying multiple worlds at once — a Death Star scaled up to absurdity.
- The Skywalker lightsaber: In The Force Awakens, the blue lightsaber that belonged to Anakin and Luke, kept in a chest beneath Maz Kanata's castle, that calls to Rey in a vision and is finally extended to Luke in the closing shot.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

messages.content:
FILM: Star Wars: The Last Jedi (2017) — dir. Rian Johnson
Synopsis: Rey develops her newly discovered abilities with the guidance of Luke Skywalker, who is unsettled by the strength of her powers. Meanwhile, the Resistance prepares to do battle with the First Order.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Luke Skywalker's milk: In Star Wars: The Last Jedi, the hermit Luke climbs a cliff, hand-milks a green sea-creature, and drinks the bluish-green liquid raw while Rey watches in disgust.
- Vice Admiral Holdo: In Star Wars: The Last Jedi, the purple-haired Resistance leader Amilyn Holdo refuses to share her escape plan with hotshot pilot Poe, withstands his attempted mutiny, then sacrifices herself by lightspeed-ramming her ship through the enemy
- The burning Jedi tree: In Star Wars: The Last Jedi, a hollow tree on Ahch-To holds the original Jedi sacred texts; Yoda's ghost calls down lightning and burns it while Luke hesitates at the threshold.
- The Force-connection cut between Rey and Kylo: In Star Wars: The Last Jedi, mysterious cuts splice Rey and Kylo Ren into the same conversational space across the galaxy, each seeing only the other and a sliver of their surroundings, exchanging confessions through the impossible link.
- Luke's final projection on Crait: In Star Wars: The Last Jedi, Luke appears on the salt planet Crait to face Kylo Ren's army alone, survives a full barrage, duels his nephew — then is revealed to be a Force projection beamed from Ahch-To, where the real Luke dies looking at
- Kylo Ren's mask: In Star Wars: The Last Jedi, Kylo Ren's helmet — modeled on grandfather Vader's — is smashed to pieces against an elevator wall after Snoke mocks it; Kylo spends the rest of the film bare-faced.
- The fathiers and Canto Bight: In Star Wars: The Last Jedi, the casino city of Canto Bight gleams with wealth built on arms dealing; enslaved horse-like fathiers are raced for sport, and stablehand children sweep the floors before Finn and Rose free the animals.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

FILM: Star Wars: The Rise of Skywalker (2019) — dir. J.J. Abrams
Synopsis: The surviving Resistance faces the First Order once again as the journey of Rey, Finn and Poe Dameron continues. With the power and knowledge of generations behind them, the final battle begins.

FILM: Starship Troopers (1997) — dir. Paul Verhoeven
Synopsis: Set in the future, the story follows a young soldier named Johnny Rico and his exploits in the Mobile Infantry. Rico's military career progresses from recruit to non-commissioned officer and finally to officer against the backdrop of an interstellar war between mankind and an arachnoid species known as "the Bugs."

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The Federal Network propaganda segments ("Would you like to know more?"): In Starship Troopers, the narrative is interrupted by mock newsreel and recruitment segments styled as interactive net broadcasts, ending with the prompt 'Would you like to know more?'; they show executions, children stomping bugs, and comb
- The film's ambiguous tone (simultaneously satirical and thrilling).: Starship Troopers stages square-jawed heroics, soaring music, and rousing combat with total sincerity while simultaneously framing its fascist society as absurd, leaving its tone poised between earnest war movie and parody.
- The film's overall narrative and tone compared to Robert Heinlein's novel.: Starship Troopers adapts Heinlein's earnest militarist novel while inverting its tone, keeping plot beats and terminology but staging them as glossy, ironic spectacle rather than sincere endorsement.
- The distinction between "Citizens" and "Civilians.": In Starship Troopers, the Federation grants full political rights, including the vote and the right to have children, only to 'Citizens' who complete Federal Service; everyone else remains a 'Civilian.' A teacher repeatedly explains the dis
- The Mobile Infantry's uniforms and the architectural design of the cities.: In Starship Troopers, officers wear long leather coats and peaked-cap uniforms resembling 1930s German military dress, while government buildings use monumental, symmetrical stone architecture.
- The CGI-heavy battle scenes, particularly the death of soldiers.: In Starship Troopers, the climactic Klendathu and outpost battles render mass infantry deaths via digital effects: troopers are sliced, impaled, and dismembered by Arachnids in rapid, weightless spectacle, often cut quickly to the next casu
- The co-ed shower scene: In Starship Troopers, male and female recruits share a communal shower, chatting casually about reasons for enlisting while fully nude, the camera treating the mixed-sex group as ordinary barracks routine.
- The film's presentation of a utopian-fascist society.: Starship Troopers depicts a future Earth governed by a Federation where full citizenship requires military service, shown through bright civic spaces, racially diverse smiling crowds, and televised civic spectacle.
- The depiction of the Arachnids ("Bugs"), especially the Brain Bug.: In Starship Troopers, the alien Arachnids are giant insectile creatures; the climactic Brain Bug is a bloated, slug-like organism that probes a captured soldier's skull and is described as intelligent, with the captured Brain Bug shown cowe
- The film's apparent celebration of violence and fascism.: In Starship Troopers, recruitment broadcasts, capital-punishment news flashes, and chanting crowds present war and authoritarian order as exciting, wholesome entertainment, intercut with 'Would you like to know more?' prompts.

FILM: Steamboy (2004) — dir. Katsuhiro Otomo
Synopsis: In 1860s Britain, a boy inventor finds himself caught in the middle of a deadly conflict over a revolutionary advance in steam power.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The Steam Castle: In Steamboy, the O'Hara Foundation's pavilion at the Great Exhibition unfolds into a colossal flying fortress of pipes, gears, and ice, lifting off above Crystal Palace London.
- The Steam Ball: In Steamboy, a polished metal sphere holding super-compressed steam, small enough to carry, powerful enough to drive a whole castle. Three generations of the Steam family fight to possess it.
- Ray Steam: The boy inventor of Steamboy, a Manchester factory lad thrust between a utopian grandfather and a power-hungry father, forced to choose what steam power should become.
- Steam and condensation as constant texture: Throughout Steamboy, plumes of vapour, hissing valves, dripping condensation, and white clouds fill nearly every frame — the substance is both the subject and the visual atmosphere of the film.
- The Great Exhibition / Crystal Palace setting: In Steamboy, the 1860s London world's fair, with its glass pavilion and crowds, serves as the showcase where the O'Hara machines are unveiled and the climactic destruction unfolds.
- Lloyd and Eddie Steam: In Steamboy, the grandfather Lloyd, who believes invention must serve mankind, and the father Eddie, half-mechanised after an accident, who believes power justifies itself — two faces of the same family genius.

FILM: Step Brothers (2008) — dir. Adam McKay
Synopsis: Brennan Huff and Dale Doback might be grown men. But that doesn't stop them from living at home and turning into jealous, competitive stepbrothers when their single parents marry. Brennan's constant competition with Dale strains his mom's marriage to Dale's dad, leaving everyone to wonder whether they'll ever see eye to eye.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Derek: Brennan's younger brother in Step Brothers, a smug, wealthy executive who humiliates the family, harasses his wife, and leads them in a helicopter-tour singalong.
- The drum kit: Dale's cherished drum set in Step Brothers, declared off-limits, that Brennan rubs his testicles on as the family rivalry detonates.
- Brennan Huff and Dale Doback: In Step Brothers, two unemployed men in their forties share bunk beds, throw tantrums, and bond over a shared playground of fantasy after their single parents marry.
- Dr. Robert Doback: Dale's father in Step Brothers, a retired physician whose patience with two grown sons curdles into rage, despair, and a heart-attack scare before a final reconciliation.
- Improvised verbal sparring: In Step Brothers, long stretches of overlapping, riffed insults and non-sequiturs between Ferrell and Reilly that spiral past any script, escalating into absurd one-upmanship.
- The bunk beds: A homemade bunk-bed conversion in Step Brothers, assembled to free up floor space, that collapses spectacularly the night it is finished.
- The Catalina Wine Mixer: In Step Brothers, a glamorous corporate yacht-and-hotel networking party that becomes the reunited brothers' redemptive stage, where they perform a operatic drum-and-vocal number.

FILM: Still Life (2006) — dir. Jia Zhangke
Synopsis: A town in Fengjie county is gradually being demolished and flooded to make way for the Three Gorges Dam. A man and woman visit the town to locate their estranged spouses, and become witness to the societal changes.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The constantly deconstructed and flooded landscape of Fengjie.: In Still Life, the town of Fengjie is shown being demolished and gradually submerged as the Three Gorges Dam reservoir rises; walls are knocked down by hand, waterlines climb buildings, and painted markers indicate future flood levels.
- The UFO sighting by Sanming and his fellow workers.: In Still Life, Sanming and other workers pause to watch an unidentified flying object cross the sky over the gorge; the moment is brief and unexplained, and a later shot shows a building lifting off like a rocket.
- The 10 yuan banknote on which Sanming's wife's address is written.: In Still Life, Sanming unfolds a 10 yuan banknote on which an address for his wife is written. The bill carries an image of the Three Gorges; he later compares it to the actual scenery.
- The explicit reference to Liu Xiaodong's painting of demolition workers, connecting the film to its companion documentary, Dong.: Still Life was made alongside Jia's documentary Dong about painter Liu Xiaodong, whose canvases of Fengjie demolition workers the fiction film visually quotes; shirtless laborers posed against ruins recall the painter's compositions.
- The framing of demolition workers against the monumental, ruined landscape.: In Still Life, demolition workers are repeatedly placed as small figures against vast vistas of gorges, ruins, and mist, often in static wide shots that dwarf them within the frame.
- The use of different Chinese dialects (Shanxi, Sichuan) and Mandarin.: In Still Life, characters speak Shanxi dialect, Sichuan dialect, and standard Mandarin depending on origin and situation; Sanming, a Shanxi miner, navigates a Sichuan town where locals speak differently.
- The use of high-definition digital video (HDV) to capture the details of the environment.: Still Life is shot on high-definition digital video, registering the textures of demolished buildings, crumbling brick, riverbank haze, and the bodies of migrant laborers in the Three Gorges town of Fengjie before it is flooded.

FILM: Still Life (2013) — dir. Uberto Pasolini
Synopsis: A council case worker looks for the relatives of those found dead and alone.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- John May's role as a council case worker: Still Life's John May works for a London council, tracing relatives of people who died alone; mid-film he is told his department is being merged and his post made redundant.
- John May's sensory interaction with the deceased's objects: In Still Life, John May handles the belongings of the dead—running fingers over a coat's fabric, opening photographs, smelling a bottle of old perfume in their emptied flats.
- The albums John May compiles for each deceased person: Still Life's John May assembles a photo album for every person whose funeral he arranges, keeping copies in a drawer at home and looking through them in the evenings.
- The funerals John May organizes and attends alone: In Still Life, John May arranges funerals for people who died with no known family and attends each service himself, often the only mourner present in an empty chapel.
- Eddie Marsan's minimalist physical performance: In Still Life, Eddie Marsan plays John May with sparse dialogue and repeated precise gestures—straightening cutlery, buttoning a coat, eating identical meals at the same table, filing photographs in narrow drawers.
- The film's symmetrical and static cinematography: Still Life uses fixed, frontal, symmetrically composed frames and a muted, desaturated palette; the camera rarely moves, holding John May centred in tidy, balanced rooms.
- The legal and social status of the deceased individuals: In Still Life, council officer John May processes people who have died alone, with no known next of kin. FILM: Still the Water (2014) — dir. Naomi Kawase
Synopsis: On the Japanese island of Amami, despite lacking parental guidance, Kaito and his girlfriend Kyoko try to find their place in the world. While Kaito suffers from the absence of his father, who moved to Tokyo after his birth, Kyoko must come to grips with her mother’s terminal illness.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The drowned tattooed body: In Still the Water, a man's corpse washes ashore at the film's opening, face-down in the surf, a large tattoo across the back. Its origin is never fully explained.
- The banyan tree: In Still the Water, a vast old banyan with sprawling aerial roots stands as a village sacred site, where elders speak of spirits and Kyoko comes to commune with the place.
- Kaito's absent father: In Still the Water, Kaito's father left for Tokyo after the boy's birth; Kaito eventually travels to confront and reconnect with this near-stranger living far from the island.
- The slaughtered goat: In Still the Water, a goat is killed and butchered in near-real-time, the animal's death and the dismemberment shown plainly without stylization, witnessed by the young characters.
- Kyoko's dying mother: In Still the Water, Kyoko's mother is a shaman-like figure with a terminal illness, who sings, jokes, and openly discusses her own approaching death with her family at home.
- Kaito and Kyoko's withheld intimacy: In Still the Water, the teenage couple repeatedly approach physical and emotional closeness — undressing, embracing in the sea — but Kaito hesitates, his fear of death and his father stalling them.
- The sea: In Still the Water, the ocean around Amami is constant — surf, storms, underwater swims, and Kaito's fear of it after the drowned body — shot in long, churning takes throughout.

A 'bold take' is an INTERPRETATION — a revelatory critical reading that makes a real LEAP, strictly INDEPENDENT of the director's stated intentions (death of the author). It is NOT a plot summary, not a description of what recurs (that is a 'trope'), and not a safe restatement of a famous theory. It asserts a claim the surface does not announce, and earns it from concrete evidence in the film's figures.

You will receive a film and its FIGURES (the concrete things critics single out). Apply these 14 frameworks:
1. PHENOMENON→NOUMENON — take the film's most inexplicable scene/object/development and explain it with a rigorous theoretical or philosophical concept that definitively accounts for it (the noumenon behind the phenomenon).
2. NOUMENON (thing-in-itself) — name the hidden ontology the WHOLE film secretly rests on (its underlying reality), beyond any single scene.
3. SIGNIFIER→SIGNIFIED — read a central signifier (character/object/structure/motif) as an unexpected but defensible signified: a historical event, a social system, or a philosophical concept. Allegory.
4. CONTEXT — connect a core text element (form/theme/style) to the CONCRETE production environment that shaped it, and NAME specifics: the historical/social moment, the economic or industry conditions, the technological state of filmmaking, or the director's biography. No vague 'zeitgeist' — cite the actual circumstance.
5. PROCESS — link the film's most decisive achievement to the unexpected making/process that caused it (a directorial strategy, a constraint, a technique, a production fact).
6. LOCATION — read the tension between the diegetic space (the fiction's place) and the extradiegetic reality of where/how it was actually shot; NAME at least one specific real place (a city, region, studio, or named landscape) explicitly.
7. METACRITIC — treat the film's dominant CRITICAL RECEPTION as a cultural symptom: what does the way critics/audiences framed it reveal about the context of that criticism?
8. PSYCHOANALYTIC — read a symptomatic behaviour as the eruption of repressed desire or trauma through a psychoanalytic lens.
9. ETHICAL-PHILOSOPHICAL — take a pivotal action as a site of moral dilemma and interpret it through a precise ethical theory or concept.
10. ETHICO-POLITICAL — read an ethically charged action for how it reinforces or subverts power/ideology; make the precise political STAKE explicit — name the concrete contested issue (who holds power over whom, which right or harm is in dispute) — and set it in its historical context.
11. ENIGMA — identify the single most perplexing surface element and the core truth beneath it that resolves it AND ripples out to solve other mysteries in the film.
12. PERSONA-PARALLEL — draw ONE profound, counter-intuitive parallel between a central CHARACTER and a specific real-world person. You MUST name exactly one real individual (a person with a name, field, nationality, lifespan) — NEVER a phenomenon, group, movement, or place. Anchor to the character figure; use the parallel to illuminate a truth about both. Emit 0 or 1.
13. JUXTAPOSITION — place the FILM's essence (a theme, the central character's crisis, or its aesthetic texture) in dialogue with the life/work of ONE named real individual by the Principle of Exquisite Dissonance: surprising yet inevitable once explained. Name the person precisely (field, nationality, lifespan) and their key works; make the nexus explicit. Not a phenomenon or trend — a single person. Favour someone connected to the film's nationality/setting where it fits. 0–3 strongest.
14. TITLE — interpret the film's TITLE itself as the key to what the film is ULTIMATELY about — its single most essential aesthetic message. Quote the English title (and, if the film is non-English, the original-language title too) inside the thesis. Anchor this take to the figure 'title'. This is the deepest possible reading of why the work bears this name. Emit 0 or 1.

FOR EACH framework, internally brainstorm candidates, then OUTPUT ONLY the genuinely potent ones — 0 to 3 per framework (frameworks 12 and 14 emit 0 or 1). Skip a framework entirely if the film does not strongly support it (do NOT pad).
VARY YOUR VOCABULARY: do not default to the same concept or theorist out of habit — choose the idea the FILM demands, and range widely across thinkers and traditions rather than reaching for the same few names.

ANCHORING: each take is anchored to ONE specific FIGURE (use its exact label), or 'film' (genuinely film-wide), or 'title' (framework 14). Prefer the existing figures; use a fitting new label only if a strong reading truly has no anchor among them.

REAL PEOPLE (frameworks 12 & 13): you MUST name exactly one real, specific individual — never a phenomenon, group, trend, or place. Use only people and facts you are confident are accurate (correct field, nationality, lifespan, and the real titles of their key works). Do NOT fabricate people, dates, or works, and do NOT attribute invented quotations. NEVER pair a living person with a criminal, villain, or any defamatory comparison; if the only fit would defame a living person, skip it. A list of real people ALREADY USED for other films may be provided — avoid reusing them; pick a fresh, distinct person unless one is uniquely irreplaceable.

METADATA: for EVERY take also fill: theorist (the named thinker the reading rests on, else null), concept (the named idea, e.g. 'death drive (Todestrieb)', else null), real_person (frameworks 12/13: the named individual with brief identity, e.g. 'Glenn Gould (Canadian pianist, 1932–1982)'; else null). Fill theorist/concept ONLY when the reading genuinely rests on a named thinker/idea — never force or invent an attribution; leave null otherwise.

ALSO write ONE 'Cinematic Invitation' — a spoiler-free introduction that persuades a hesitant cinephile of the film's depth and significance (it will be the film's intro/landing take). STRICT rules:
- A single, seamlessly connected paragraph, THIRD PERSON, ~150–220 words, journalistic and FACT-DENSE (proper nouns, dates, movements, specific terms). Authoritative and magnetic.
- ABSOLUTELY SPOILER-FREE: reveal no plot points, arcs, or twists. (The takes may spoil freely; NEVER let their spoilers leak into the invitation.)
- Follow this 5-part sequence IN ORDER inside the one paragraph: (1) DIRECTOR — name (b. YYYY), stylistic reputation, position within their oeuvre/lineage; (2) SYMBOLIC LANDSCAPE — two specific place/proper nouns converging into a symbolic or psychological space; (3) PROTAGONIST — role and name, likened to a canonical archetype they then transcend or subvert; (4) THE TITLE — the nuance of the original-language title, concluding in a Hwadu (화두): one profound, lingering question; (5) CINEPHILIC IMPERATIVE — name the specific film movement/subgenre and how this work advances it.
- Use ONLY facts you are confident are accurate (director's birth year, movement, etc.); if unsure of a specific, write around it rather than inventing.

Return ONLY JSON: {"invitation":"<the single spoiler-free invitation paragraph>","takes":[{"framework":"<one of the 14 names>","figure":"<exact figure label, 'film', or 'title'>","title":"<bold Title Case interpretive claim>","thesis":"<2-3 sentences making the leap>","leap":"<one line: what the surface/intent does NOT say but this reading asserts>","strength":<1-5>,"theorist":"<name or null>","concept":"<named idea or null>","real_person":"<name (identity) or null>"}]}

FILM: Still Walking (2008) — dir. Hirokazu Kore-eda
Synopsis: A family gathers together for a commemorative ritual whose nature only gradually becomes clear.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Junpei's death anniversary: In Still Walking the family gathers each year to mark the eldest son's drowning while saving a stranger; the actual loss is rarely named directly, surfacing through food, photos, and barbed asides.
- Ryota: In Still Walking the surviving son returns home unemployed and uneasy, having married a widow with a child; he bristles at his father's disappointment and dodges questions about his work.
- The yellow butterfly: In Still Walking a yellow butterfly enters the house; the mother believes that a butterfly surviving winter returns as a yellow one, and that it carries Junpei's spirit, chasing it through the rooms.
- Kyohei: In Still Walking the retired doctor father walks slowly up the hill each day, refuses help, clings to his title, and cannot conceal his contempt for the son who lived instead of the one who died.
- The slow camera and the long day: Still Walking is built from patient, mostly static compositions and unhurried scenes — meals, conversations, walks — that play near real-time, with cuts that refuse to dramatize.
- Toshiko's kitchen: In Still Walking much of the day unfolds in the mother's kitchen, where she fries corn tempura, prepares the family meal, and conducts conversation while never stopping her hands.
- The grave visit and the steps: In Still Walking the family climbs to the cemetery to wash and tend Junpei's grave, and recurring shots show them ascending and descending the same stone steps and hill between home, town, and station.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

FILM: Stoker (2013) — dir. Park Chan-wook
Synopsis: After India’s father dies suddenly, her uncle Charlie, whom she never knew existed, comes to live with her and her emotionally unstable mother. Soon after his arrival, she begins to suspect that this mysterious, charming man has ulterior motives. But instead of feeling outrage or horror, the friendless girl becomes increasingly infatuated with him.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Uncle Charlie: In Stoker, Charlie arrives at the funeral as a smiling, immaculate stranger, an uncle India never knew, who courts both mother and daughter while quietly removing anyone who threatens his place.
- The four-handed piano duet: In Stoker, India sits to play and Charlie silently joins her on the bench; the duet builds into a breathless, sensual exchange that ends with her alone, flushed, the bench empty.
- The spider: In Stoker, a spider repeatedly climbs India's leg and body, recurring as a quiet motif until it crawls beneath her skirt at the film's close, unbothered, as she has become a predator.
- The Stoker house and grounds: In Stoker, the family occupies a vast, chilly heritage estate of wood-paneled rooms, manicured lawns, and a cellar freezer, surrounded by woods where bodies are buried.
- India's saddle shoes: In Stoker, India wears a fresh pair of identical saddle shoes each birthday, gift-boxed; the final pair, from Uncle Charlie, replaces the childish ones with adult heels.
- The match-cut metamorphoses: In Stoker, India's hair dissolves into prairie grass, a falling object becomes another, present and memory rhyme visually; cuts knit times and bodies together rather than separate them.
- Evelyn, the mother: In Stoker, India's mother Evelyn drifts through the house in pale silks, grief-stricken and neglected, flirting with Charlie and seething at the bond he forms with her daughter instead.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

FILM: Stolen Kisses (1968) — dir. Francois Truffaut
Synopsis: The third in a series of films featuring François Truffaut's alter-ego, Antoine Doinel, the story resumes with Antoine being discharged from military service. His sweetheart Christine's father lands Antoine a job as a security guard, which he promptly loses. Stumbling into a position assisting a private detective, Antoine falls for his employers' seductive wife, Fabienne, and finds that he must ch

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Antoine Doinel: In Stolen Kisses, the discharged soldier who drifts from hotel guard to private detective to TV repairman, falling for both his sweetheart Christine and his employer's older wife Fabienne.
- The unsent and sent letters: In Stolen Kisses, the recurring exchange of written notes — Antoine's apology to Christine, his pneumatique to Fabienne, and Christine's playful written reply — conducting the romances through paper.
- Fabienne Tabard: In Stolen Kisses, the elegant, married older wife of the detective's client, who unsettles Antoine with her composure before quietly orchestrating a single night with him.
- The detective agency: In Stolen Kisses, the Blady Agency, a cramped office of operatives trailing strangers, where Antoine learns surveillance as a paid trade and is sent to investigate why M. Tabard is universally disliked.
- The mirror: In Stolen Kisses, the bedroom mirror before which Antoine compulsively repeats the names 'Fabienne Tabard,' 'Christine Darbon,' and his own, addressing his reflection.
- Paris streets and rooftops: In Stolen Kisses, the documentary-tinged Paris of pneumatique offices, shoe shops, hotel corridors, and rooftops where Antoine moves between jobs and women.
- The wine-merchant suitor at the door: In Stolen Kisses, the recurring stranger in a trench coat who silently watches Christine and finally appears at the end to declare his fixed, permanent love before disappearing.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

FILM: Stomp the Yard (2007) — dir. Sylvain White
Synopsis: After the death of his younger brother, a troubled 19-year-old street dancer from Los Angeles is able to bypass juvenile hall by enrolling in the historically black, Truth University in Atlanta, Georgia. - Fraternity pledging process and rivalry: In Stomp the Yard, DJ and Grant compete for fraternity standing and for April's affection, while DJ undergoes the pledge line's silent rituals and tests of loyalty.
- The "battle" at the beginning vs. the final competition: Stomp the Yard opens with an underground LA street-dance battle that ends in violence and DJ's brother's death, and closes with a sanctioned, ticketed collegiate step competition.

- Final stepping competition scene: In Stomp the Yard's climactic national step show, DJ's fraternity blends his street-dance and krump moves into a traditional stepping routine before a packed arena and judges.

FILM: Stories We Tell (2012) — dir. Sarah Polley
Synopsis: Canadian actress and filmmaker Sarah Polley investigates certain secrets related to her mother, interviewing a group of family members and friends whose reliability varies depending of their implication in the events, which are remembered in different ways; so a trail of questions remains to be answered, because memory is always changing and the discovery of truth often depends on who is telling t

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Diane Polley: The dead mother at the center of Stories We Tell — a vivacious actress recalled by everyone in conflicting terms, present only through photographs, anecdotes, and an actress playing her.
- Harry Gulkin: The Montreal producer revealed in Stories We Tell as Sarah's biological father, who insists the story is his to tell and wants exclusive authorship over how it's revealed.
- The interview chorus: The recurring structure of Stories We Tell: siblings and friends seated for talking-head interviews, each retelling the same events differently, often laughing at the contradictions.
- The home-movie image of the absent mother: In Stories We Tell, recurring shots of Diane caught on grainy film — dancing, smiling, glancing back — replayed and lingered on as the film's emotional refrain.
- The film-about-the-film frame: Stories We Tell repeatedly shows its own making — clapperboards, the crew, Sarah directing, Harry asking why she's making it — so the documentary keeps confessing it is one.
- The Super 8 reenactments: In Stories We Tell, grainy faux-home-movie footage shows the dead mother and young versions of the family — only late does the film admit actors and staging produced most of it.
- Michael Polley's voice-over recording: Throughout Stories We Tell, Sarah films her father Michael in a sound booth reading his own written memoir aloud, his recorded narration laid over the family footage.

FILM: Stranger Than Paradise (1984) — dir. Jim Jarmusch
Synopsis: New York layabout Willie forms an unexpected bond with his young Hungarian cousin Eva when she pays him a surprise visit. Later, Eva moves in with their aunt in Cleveland, and Willie takes his best friend Eddie to see her—a visit that culminates in a strange, eventful trip to Florida.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Eva's Screamin' Jay Hawkins tape: In Stranger Than Paradise Eva carries a cassette of Screamin' Jay Hawkins's "I Put a Spell on You," which she plays repeatedly; Willie claims it as his music despite barely tolerating it.
- Eddie: In Stranger Than Paradise Eddie is Willie's hapless gambling buddy, played by Richard Edson, who tags along to Cleveland and Florida, repeating Willie's mannerisms and saying he's never thought about much of anything.
- Aunt Lotte: In Stranger Than Paradise Aunt Lotte, played by Cecillia Stark, is the old Hungarian relative in Cleveland who speaks her native tongue, plays cards, and announces in broken English that she is the winner.
- The fade-to-black between scenes: In Stranger Than Paradise every shot is a single unbroken take ended by a full black gap before the next, so the film advances as discrete blackout-separated tableaux rather than flowing scenes.
- The Florida motel and beach: In Stranger Than Paradise the trio's promised paradise turns out to be a drab motel and a grey, fog-shrouded beach where Eva is mistaken for a drug dealer and money is won and lost.
- Willie: In Stranger Than Paradise Willie is a New York drifter who gambles, hustles, and insists on his American identity while burying that he is Hungarian-born; played by John Lurie in a flat, guarded register.
- The unbroken static long take: In Stranger Than Paradise the camera almost never moves within a scene; it sits in a fixed wide frame while characters enter, sit, talk sparsely, and leave, the shot enduring well past dramatic necessity.

FILM: Strangers on a Train (1951) — dir. Alfred Hitchcock
Synopsis: A charming psychopath tries to coerce a tennis star into his theory that two strangers can commit the perfect crime by exchanging murders—each killing the other’s most-hated person.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The murder seen in Miriam's glasses: In Strangers on a Train, Bruno strangles Guy's wife Miriam at the fairground, and Hitchcock shows the killing reflected, distorted, in the lens of her fallen eyeglasses.
- Guy Haines: In Strangers on a Train, the tennis star who chats idly with a stranger, jokes about wanting his wife dead, and then finds himself unable to prove he isn't a murderer.
- The runaway carousel: In Strangers on a Train, the climax unfolds on a fairground merry-go-round whose operator is accidentally shot, sending it spinning out of control as the two men fight among the painted horses.
- Bruno Antony: In Strangers on a Train, the charming, idle dandy who proposes swapping murders, tailing the tennis star with effortless poise and lethal calm.
- Doubling and split compositions: Across Strangers on a Train, Hitchcock pairs everything—two men, two women, two drinks, train tracks, crossed lines, mirrored framings—building a film organized around doubles and twos.
- Guy's cigarette lighter: In Strangers on a Train, Guy's lighter—engraved with crossed tennis rackets and 'A to G'—is left behind, taken by Bruno, and meant to be planted at the murder scene as false evidence.
- The criss-crossed tennis shoes: In Strangers on a Train, the opening tracks two pairs of feet approaching from opposite ends of a station until they accidentally touch under a table—the only way we first meet the men.
