FILM: The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2011) — dir. David Fincher
Synopsis: Disgraced journalist Mikael Blomkvist investigates the disappearance of a weary patriarch's niece from 40 years ago. He is aided by the pierced, tattooed, punk computer hacker named Lisbeth Salander. As they work together in the investigation, Blomkvist and Salander uncover immense corruption beyond anything they have ever imagined.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Bjurman's rape and the hidden camera: In The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, the recurring device of recorded evidence: Bjurman's assault, secretly filmed, becomes the leverage Salander uses to control him afterward.
- Hedeby Island and the Vanger estate: In The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, the snowbound private island where the Vanger clan live in separate houses across one bridge, the site of Harriet's 40-year-old disappearance.
- Martin Vanger: In The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, the affable, successful CEO of the Vanger group whose polished hospitality conceals a soundproofed basement where he tortures and kills women.
- Lisbeth Salander: In The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, the pierced, tattooed hacker and ward of the state who investigates, hacks, avenges, and brands her assailant. Black clothes, blunt affect, photographic recall.
- The Reznor-Ross score: The Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross score for The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo: low synth drones, glassy industrial textures, and a thudding cover of 'Immigrant Song' over the title sequence.
- The title sequence: The black-oil opening of The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo: abstract tar-coated bodies, keyboards, cables, and a dragon fusing and dissolving in fluid CG, scored to the screaming 'Immigrant Song' cover.
- The case files and photographs: In The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, the decades-old archive Blomkvist works through: Harriet's pressed flowers, the parade photographs, the Bible-verse notebook of names, and Martin's hidden trophy images.

FILM: The Girl with the Needle (2024) — dir. Magnus von Horn
Synopsis: Struggling to survive in post-WWI Copenhagen, a newly unemployed and pregnant young woman is taken in by a charismatic elder to help run an underground adoption agency. The two form an unexpected bond, until a sudden discovery changes everything.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The surviving girl: In The Girl with the Needle, the one small child Dagmar keeps rather than kills — her own household ward — drifts silently through the candy shop, witness to a trade she cannot name. Erena, played as a near-mute presence.
- Dagmar: The warm, motherly proprietor of a candy shop in The Girl with the Needle who runs a clandestine adoption service, taking money to place unwanted babies — and quietly killing them. Trine Dyrholm plays her with disarming tenderness.
- Karoline: In The Girl with the Needle, the young pregnant seamstress drifts from factory floor to brothel to candy shop, surviving by attaching herself to whoever will take her in. Her hollow stare and clenched composure rarely break.
- The candy / ether: In The Girl with the Needle, sweets and a sedative haze recur as substances of consolation: candy quiets the surviving child, ether dulls the women's despair. Both numb without nourishing.
- The monochrome chiaroscuro: The Girl with the Needle is shot entirely in high-contrast black and white, faces emerging from and dissolving into deep shadow, the cold grey of Copenhagen rendered like an etching or a silent-era frame.
- Peter's scarred face: In The Girl with the Needle, Karoline's missing husband returns from the war with a grotesquely disfigured face, later concealed behind a mask and exhibited as a sideshow attraction. His wound is the war made visible on flesh.
- The candy shop: The cramped, dimly lit sweet shop in The Girl with the Needle where Dagmar sells confections to children by day and receives unwanted infants by the same counter. Jars of bright candy line shelves above the killing.

FILM: The Gleaners and I (2000) — dir. Agnes Varda
Synopsis: Varda focuses her eye on gleaners: those who scour already-reaped fields for the odd potato or turnip. Her investigation leads from forgotten corners of the French countryside to off-hours at the green markets of Paris, following those who insist on finding a use for that which society has cast off, whether out of necessity or activism.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The recovered clock without hands: Near the end of The Gleaners and I, Varda finds and keeps a discarded mantel clock that has no hands, placing it on a shelf and filming herself moving behind it.
- Varda's aging hands: In The Gleaners and I, Varda turns the camera on her own wrinkled hand, filming it with the other, and later films her grey hair in close-up. She frames her body as one more thing the world discards.
- The heart-shaped potatoes: In The Gleaners and I, Varda discovers and collects misshapen potatoes shaped like hearts, rejected by supermarkets for being non-standard. She keeps them, films them, and watches them sprout.
- The handheld digital camera: The Gleaners and I is shot on a small consumer digital camera Varda carries herself, producing intimate, sometimes shaky, often improvised footage including an accidental shot of the lens cap dancing on its strap.
- The Jean-François Millet painting: The Gleaners and I opens with Millet's 1857 painting 'The Gleaners' in a dictionary and a museum, women bent in fields; Varda returns to this and other paintings of gleaners as the film's historical anchor.
- The urban gleaners at market's end: In The Gleaners and I, Varda follows people who collect discarded produce and goods after Paris markets close — among them a young man who eats only from bins yet teaches immigrants to read at night.
- The framed-hands gesture toward passing trucks: In The Gleaners and I, Varda playfully frames passing highway trucks between her thumb and finger as if catching them, a recurring gesture of grasping at fleeting things from her car window.

FILM: The Goddess (1934) — dir. Wu Yonggang
Synopsis: A young prostitute, who is trying to give her infant son a good start in life, must contend with a coercive pimp and the prejudices of others.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The pimp / the boss: In The Goddess, a heavyset gambler attaches himself to the woman, pockets her earnings, blocks the door when she tries to leave, and lounges while she works.
- The son: In The Goddess, the infant grows into a small boy in school uniform; he cannot grasp his mother's life and exists as the silent reason for all her sacrifice.
- The held close-up of Ruan's face: In The Goddess, Wu repeatedly holds on Ruan Lingyu's face in tight close-up — watching her son, enduring the pimp, sitting in her cell — letting the silent performance carry meaning words cannot.
- The Goddess (the unnamed mother): In The Goddess, a young woman works the night streets and raises her infant son by day, her two lives never named, only shown through dress, posture, and the turn of her head.
- The streetlamp and the legs: In The Goddess, the woman's solicitation is conveyed by a recurring low shot: her legs framed beneath a glowing streetlamp, a man's shadow approaching, the act itself elided.
- The hidden money: In The Goddess, the mother tucks her savings into a hole in the brick wall, money meant for the boy's schooling — until the pimp discovers and gambles it away.
- The kindly schoolmaster: In The Goddess, an elderly headmaster defends the boy's right to study, visits the mother's home, and ultimately resigns when the board expels the child — vowing to raise him himself.

FILM: The Godfather (1972) — dir. Francis Ford Coppola
Synopsis: Spanning the years 1945 to 1955, a chronicle of the fictional Italian-American Corleone crime family. Don Vito conducts murder negotiations in a study hung with family photos, and the climactic christening is intercut with 
- Michael Corleone's character arc from war hero to ruthless Don.: In The Godfather, Michael Corleone first appears in military uniform telling Kay his family's business is not his own, then progressively kills Sollozzo and the police captain, takes over operations, and by the end is addressed as Don, the 
- The baptism scene, intercut with the assassinations of the heads of the Five Families.: In The Godfather, Michael stands as godfather at his nephew's church baptism, answering the priest's questions about renouncing Satan, while the film cuts to his men carrying out simultaneous murders of rival bosses.
- The depiction of Italian-American cultural traditions (food, weddings, family gatherings).: In The Godfather, the film opens on Connie's lavish wedding with dancing, singing, and abundant food, and returns to scenes of cooking, shared meals, and family rituals throughout.
- The exclusion of female characters, especially Kay, from the family's inner sanctum.: In The Godfather, women are repeatedly sent out of rooms where business is discussed, and the final shot shows Kay watching through a doorway as men kiss Michael's hand before the door is closed in her face.
- The use of darkness and underexposure in Gordon Willis's cinematography.: In The Godfather, interiors are lit from overhead so Don Vito's eyes fall into shadow, and many scenes sit at the edge of underexposure. Outdoor Sicily and the wedding scenes appear bright by contrast; indoor power scenes go nearly black.
- The Corleone family's business operations and structure.: In The Godfather, the Corleones run gambling, unions, and political favors through a hierarchy of Don, consigliere, and capos, holding meetings about market territory, mergers with other families, and whether to enter the narcotics trade.

Synopsis: In the continuing saga of the Corleone crime family, a young Vito Corleone grows up in Sicily and in 1910s New York. In the 1950s, Michael Corleone attempts to expand the family business into Las Vegas, Hollywood and Cuba.

FILM: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly (1966) — dir. Sergio Leone
Synopsis: While the Civil War rages on between the Union and the Confederacy, three men – a quiet loner, a ruthless hitman, and a Mexican bandit – comb the American Southwest in search of a strongbox containing $200,000 in stolen gold.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The desert march: In The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, Tuco forces a captured Blondie to walk across a blistering desert without water, repeated when the roles reverse — bodies burnt, lips cracked, faces blistering in the sun, shot in punishing wide stillness.
- Morricone's three-note theme: Ennio Morricone's main theme for The Good, the Bad and the Ugly — a coyote-howl phrase doubled by whistles, ocarina, electric guitar and voices, with a distinct sonic signature assigned to each of the three men.
- Tuco: The 'Ugly' of The Good, the Bad and the Ugly — a Mexican bandit, played by Eli Wallach, who talks constantly, double-crosses Blondie repeatedly, prays, weeps, and survives by sheer scrambling cunning.
- The Civil War as backdrop: Throughout The Good, the Bad and the Ugly, the treasure hunt unfolds against the American Civil War — a prison camp, a shelled town, and a pointless battle over a bridge that the three protagonists treat as an obstacle, not a cause.

FILM: The Goonies (1985) — dir. Richard Donner
Synopsis: Young teen Mikey Walsh and his friends set off on a quest to find Pirate One-Eyed Willie's treasure in hopes of saving their homes from demolition. However, on their quest to find the treasure, they run into a family of recently escaped criminals, determined to capture the kids and reach the treasure first.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The central plot conflict: the foreclosure of the Goon Docks: In The Goonies, the kids' homes face demolition because their parents cannot meet mortgage payments to the country club developers; the signed foreclosure papers drive the hunt for One-Eyed Willy's treasure.
- The character of Sloth: In The Goonies, Sloth is a large, facially deformed Fratelli brother kept chained in the basement, who befriends Chunk over candy and turns against his cruel family to help the children.
- The collective group of male Goonies: In The Goonies, the central gang — Mikey, Brand, Mouth, Chunk, and Data — bicker, taunt each other, and pledge loyalty as 'Goonies' while navigating the underground caves together.
- The film's overall audiovisual aesthetic (lighting, score, pacing): The Goonies pairs warm, adventure-serial lighting and cavern shadows with Dave Grusin's swelling orchestral score and a relentless, breathless cutting pace that rarely lets a scene settle.
- The subterranean network of caves and tunnels: In The Goonies, the kids descend through a restaurant basement into an elaborate underground of booby-trapped tunnels, an underground river, skeletons, and One-Eyed Willy's buried pirate galleon.
- The film's enduring cult status and fan community: The Goonies sustains a devoted fan culture decades on — reunions, anniversary screenings, location pilgrimages to Astoria, Oregon, and merchandise — built largely on viewers who first saw it as children.

FILM: The Gospel According to St. Matthew (1965) — dir. Pier Paolo Pasolini
Synopsis: Along a rocky, barren coastline, Jesus begins teaching, primarily using parables. He attracts disciples; he's stern, brusque, and demanding. His parables often take on the powers that be, so he and his teachings come to the attention of the Pharisees, the chief priests, and elders. They conspire to have him arrested, beaten, tried, and crucified, just as he prophesied to his followers.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Enrique Irazoqui's Jesus: In The Gospel According to St. Matthew, a young, dark-browed Jesus delivers parables with a clenched stare, often striding ahead of his disciples or turning back to address the camera mid-walk. His tone is curt, his face rarely softens.
- The borrowed-music score: In The Gospel According to St. Matthew, the soundtrack collages Bach's Mass and Passions, Mozart, a Congolese Missa Luba, Odetta singing 'Sometimes I Feel Like a Motherless Child,' and Russian and folk fragments — none composed for the film
- Susanna Pasolini's aged Mary: In The Gospel According to St. Matthew, the older Mary at the crucifixion is played by Pasolini's own mother, her lined face crumpling in silent grief beneath the cross. She speaks almost nothing; her anguish is entirely facial.
- The walking-and-talking tracking shots: In The Gospel According to St. Matthew, Jesus frequently delivers teaching while striding across open country, the handheld camera trailing or flanking him, sometimes losing focus, his words tumbling out as the group moves through dust and 
- The Pharisees and elders: In The Gospel According to St. Matthew, the religious authorities appear in ornate ceremonial dress and tall headgear, often grouped on temple steps, conferring in shadow to plot Jesus's arrest. They are the only figures whose costume reads
- The rocky barren coastline: The Gospel According to St. Matthew unfolds across the dry hills, caves, and stony slopes of Southern Italy. Sites stand in for Galilee and Jerusalem — no temples, no marble, just eroded rock, dust, and a few mud-brick walls.

FILM: The Graduate (1967) — dir. Mike Nichols
Synopsis: A disillusioned college graduate finds himself torn between his older lover and her daughter.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Simon & Garfunkel's 'The Sound of Silence': In The Graduate, the song recurs over Benjamin's wordless drifting — gliding the airport walkway at the start, floating on the pool raft, walking corridors — as a continuous, melancholy commentary.
- The Taft Hotel rooms: In The Graduate, the affair plays out in anonymous, beige hotel rooms where Benjamin signs in nervously and the lovers undress in clinical silence, the TV sometimes on.
- Benjamin Braddock: In The Graduate, the recently returned college star, awkward and inarticulate, drifts through his parents' expectations, the affair, and finally a desperate pursuit of Elaine across California.
- Glass between Ben and Elaine: In The Graduate, recurring panes separate Benjamin from what he wants: he pounds on the glass wall of the church balcony screaming Elaine's name before they flee together.
- The fish tank and diving suit: In The Graduate, Benjamin watches the world through aquarium glass in his bedroom, then is sealed into a black scuba suit and lowered into the pool at his parents' party while guests applaud.
- Mrs. Robinson: In The Graduate, the wife of Mr. Robinson seduces the much-younger Benjamin, conducts the affair in clinical hotel rooms, and turns vicious when he pursues her daughter.
- The final bus shot: In The Graduate, Ben and Elaine, breathless and laughing, board a city bus after the wedding escape; Nichols holds the camera as their elated grins slowly fade into uncertain blankness.

FILM: The Grand Budapest Hotel (2014) — dir. Wes Anderson
Synopsis: The Grand Budapest Hotel tells of a legendary concierge at a famous European hotel between the wars and his friendship with a young employee who becomes his trusted protégé. The story involves the theft and recovery of a priceless Renaissance painting, the battle for an enormous family fortune and the slow and then sudden upheavals that transformed Europe during the first half of the 20th century.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The film's blend of melancholic comedy and historical tragedy.: In The Grand Budapest Hotel, brisk slapstick chases and deadpan one-liners share scenes with executions, a war, and the murder of side characters announced in flat title-card postscripts.
- The film's meticulous production design and focus on objects (e.g., Mendl's pastries, the painting 'Boy with Apple').: The Grand Budapest Hotel lingers on hand-crafted props: Mendl's pink Courtesan au Chocolat boxes tied with ribbon, and the Renaissance panel 'Boy with Apple,' stolen, hidden, and swapped for a lewd painting.
- The film's overall aesthetic of artifice (symmetrical compositions, frontality, theatrical sets).: The Grand Budapest Hotel composes nearly every shot dead-center and symmetrical, with characters facing the camera, whip-pans between them, and sets that read as painted flats and obvious miniatures.
- The mentorship relationship between M. Gustave and Zero Moustafa.: In The Grand Budapest Hotel, the perfumed concierge M. Gustave takes the refugee lobby boy Zero under his wing, drilling him in service, sharing poetry, and ultimately dying to defend him.
- The use of miniatures and dioramic visuals (e.g., the hotel exterior, the funicular).: The Grand Budapest Hotel renders its exterior, the funicular climbing the slope, and a cable-car chase as visibly handmade models — painted backdrops, scale buildings, and toy-like vehicles moving in shallow space.
- The film's self-conscious anachronisms and "model-making" aesthetic.: The Grand Budapest Hotel renders its hotel, funicular, and snowbound chases as visible scale models and stop-motion miniatures, with deliberately imprecise period detail across its nested historical frames.
- The film's depiction of a lost, idealized pre-war European civilization (Zubrowka).: The Grand Budapest Hotel sets its action in Zubrowka, a fictional alpine republic with invented currency, borders, and a hotel whose grandeur is shown fading across nested timeframes toward Soviet-era drabness.
- The nested narrative structure (story within a story within a story).: In The Grand Budapest Hotel, the story passes through frames: a girl at a writer's grave, the elderly Author addressing a camera, his younger self interviewing Zero, and finally Gustave's tale. Each layer shifts aspect ratio and decade.

FILM: The Great Beauty (2013) — dir. Paolo Sorrentino
Synopsis: Jep Gambardella has seduced his way through the lavish nightlife of Rome for decades, but after his 65th birthday and a shock from the past, Jep looks past the nightclubs and parties to find a timeless landscape of absurd, exquisite beauty.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Jep Gambardella: In The Great Beauty, the aging socialite-novelist who wrote one acclaimed book decades ago, now hosts and dismantles Rome's nightlife with practiced charm and a cigarette permanently lit.
- Rome itself: Rome in The Great Beauty appears at dawn and night as a gliding succession of fountains, ruins, terraces and empty piazzas, shot in fluid crane and tracking moves that treat the city as the film's true subject.
- The Saint (Sister Maria): In The Great Beauty, an ancient, near-mummified missionary nun revered as a living saint, who eats only roots, sleeps on the floor, and climbs the Scala Santa on her knees.
- Ramona's striptease: In The Great Beauty, the 42-year-old stripper Ramona, daughter of Jep's friend, performs in clubs and forms a tender, sexless companionship with Jep before quietly dying of an undisclosed illness.
- The conga line and party choreography: In The Great Beauty, rooftop parties dissolve into pulsing dance sequences, slow-motion crowds, thumping electronica and a recurring human conga line that Jep proudly calls the best in Rome because it never goes anywhere.
- Elisa, the first love: In The Great Beauty, Jep's adolescent first love whose recent death — revealed by her widower visiting Jep — triggers the whole film, surfacing in luminous flashbacks of a seaside cliff and a girl half-undressing in moonlight.
- The performance artist / child painter set-pieces: In The Great Beauty, the contemporary-art world is skewered in episodes: a nude performance artist headbutting a Roman aqueduct, and a child made to hurl paint at a canvas before a paying crowd, weeping as she works.

FILM: The Green Knight (2021) — dir. David Lowery
Synopsis: An epic fantasy adventure based on the timeless Arthurian legend, The Green Knight tells the story of Sir Gawain, King Arthur's reckless and headstrong nephew, who embarks on a daring quest to confront the eponymous Green Knight, a gigantic emerald-skinned stranger and tester of men.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The Lady: In The Green Knight, the lord's wife at the manor near the chapel, played by Alicia Vikander, who mirrors Gawain's earlier lover, seduces and unnerves him, and delivers the girdle alongside a speech on the color green.
- The Green Knight: In The Green Knight, the bark-skinned, branch-antlered visitor who rides into Camelot, offers a Christmas game, takes Gawain's blow, and retrieves his own severed head to depart laughing.
- The talking fox: In The Green Knight, the fox that joins Gawain on the road, travels with him through the wilderness, and finally speaks in warning, urging him to turn back from the chapel before he loses everything.
- The imagined future: In The Green Knight, the long wordless sequence in which Gawain envisions fleeing the blow — returning home, taking a crown, abandoning a lover, raising a son lost to war, and dying as his court collapses around him.
- The slow circling camera: In The Green Knight, the recurring 360-degree pans and unhurried tracking moves — most strikingly the rotation around Gawain bound on the forest floor that shifts him to a skeleton — that survey scenes at a deliberate, ritual pace.
- The green girdle: In The Green Knight, the green silk sash Gawain's mother gives him and later receives again from the Lady, said to protect its wearer from harm; he clings to it on the road to the chapel.
- The Green Chapel: In The Green Knight, the moss-grown, half-flooded ruin at the end of Gawain's quest, where the Green Knight sleeps until the appointed day and where the final blow is owed.

FILM: The Green Mile (1999) — dir. Frank Darabont
Synopsis: A supernatural tale set on death row in a Southern prison, where gentle giant John Coffey possesses the mysterious power to heal people's ailments. When the cell block's head guard, Paul Edgecomb, recognizes Coffey's miraculous gift, he tries desperately to help stave off the condemned man's execution.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Character of John Coffey: In The Green Mile, John Coffey is a towering Black death-row inmate who heals a guard's bladder infection, revives a crushed mouse, and weeps absorbing others' pain. He fears the dark and asks no mercy at his execution.
- Film's narrative structure compared to the serialized novel: The Green Mile adapts Stephen King's six-part serialized novel into a single three-hour film, framed as the elderly Paul Edgecomb recounting the story from a nursing home decades later.
- The film's emotional argument against capital punishment: The Green Mile depicts executions in extended detail, including Del's botched electrocution where the dry sponge causes prolonged burning, and ends with the guards executing the innocent, miracle-working Coffey.
- The film's generic hybridity: The Green Mile combines a 1930s prison drama, supernatural fantasy, courtroom-tinged mystery, and weepie melodrama, set within a Depression-era penitentiary and framed by a nursing-home memory.
- The flashback framing device (Elderly Paul Edgecomb): The Green Mile opens and closes with an aged Paul Edgecomb in a retirement home, recounting the 1935 events to a fellow resident. The final scenes reveal he is unnaturally long-lived, attending the funerals of everyone he has outlasted.
- Thomas Newman's non-diegetic musical score: In The Green Mile, Thomas Newman's score layers soft piano, sustained strings, and shimmering tones beneath key scenes — John Coffey's healings, the executions, and Paul's narration — swelling at moments of suffering and grace.
- Character of Percy Wetmore: Percy Wetmore is a young guard at Cold Mountain penitentiary in The Green Mile who is protected by family ties to the governor. He sabotages an execution by withholding the sponge's water, taunts prisoners, and stomps a pet mouse.
- John Coffey's narrative arc (healing, suffering, sacrifice): In The Green Mile, John Coffey heals the sick, revives the dead mouse, takes others' afflictions into himself, is executed though innocent, and bears the initials J.C. His arc moves through miracle, suffering, and death.
- The film's setting and atmosphere (1930s Louisiana prison): In The Green Mile, the action unfolds almost entirely within a 1930s Louisiana death-row block, lit in warm amber and brown, with a sweating warden's office, a restraint room, and the electric chair at the corridor's end. FILM: The Green Ray (1986) — dir. Eric Rohmer
Synopsis: A lonely Parisian woman comes to terms with her isolation and anxieties during a long summer vacation.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The failed vacations: In The Green Ray, Delphine cycles through borrowed and improvised holidays — a friend's family flat, the mountains, Cherbourg, Biarritz — abandoning each almost as she arrives, unable to settle anywhere.
- Marie Rivière's improvised performance: In The Green Ray, Marie Rivière co-developed her dialogue with Rohmer, performing Delphine in a hesitant, self-interrupting, documentary-real register rather than polished scripted speech.
- The overheard conversations: In The Green Ray, Delphine is repeatedly placed at the edge of group talk — beach chatter, terrace debates, family banter — listening more than speaking, often filmed slightly apart from the speakers.
- The green ray itself: In The Green Ray, the title refers to a rare optical flash at the horizon as the sun sets; Delphine overhears it described as a sign that lets you read your own and others' hearts, and waits the whole film to see it.
- The playing card on the ground: In The Green Ray, Delphine begins finding playing cards lying in the street and treats them as omens, reading their suits as messages addressed to her wandering summer.
- Delphine's tears: In The Green Ray, Delphine weeps repeatedly and almost involuntarily — at a dinner table, in a field, on benches — often unable to explain why, drawing irritated or baffled responses from companions.
- Delphine's vegetarianism: In The Green Ray, Delphine repeatedly explains and defends her refusal to eat meat over meals, drawing skeptical, faintly mocking interrogation from the people around her.

FILM: The Hand of God (2021) — dir. Paolo Sorrentino
Synopsis: In 1980s Naples, an awkward teen struggling to find his place experiences heartbreak and liberation after he's inadvertently saved from a freak accident by football legend Diego Maradona.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The director Capuano's tirade: Near the end of The Hand of God, the volatile filmmaker Antonio Capuano berates Fabietto on a city street, demanding he find something to say and refuse self-pity, in effect handing him the call to make films.
- The mother's juggled oranges: In The Hand of God, Fabietto's mother juggles oranges and plays elaborate pranks; the small domestic trick recurs as her signature before the gas-leak deaths.
- The 'little monk' folk spirit: In The Hand of God the recurring superstition of the 'munaciello,' a small monk-like household sprite said to bring fortune or children, threads through the family's beliefs, especially around Patrizia.
- The 'Capri-Maradona' Naples: The Hand of God shoots 1980s Naples as a layered character — alleyways, the bay, balconies, the football-mad crowd, the noise and superstition of the city woven through every scene.
- Maradona's deferred presence: Throughout The Hand of God, Diego Maradona is talked about, glimpsed on television, and credited with saving Fabietto, but the actual man stays almost entirely off-screen. His transfer to Napoli organizes the whole family's hope.
- The seaside summer house: In The Hand of God the extended family gathers at a coastal villa for sun, food, swimming and bickering. It is where the parents are happiest and where, later, their absence is felt most sharply.
- Aunt Patrizia: In The Hand of God, the beautiful, troubled Patrizia sunbathes nude on the family boat, claims to have met a saint, and is institutionalized. She is the object of Fabietto's adolescent fixation.

FILM: The Handmaiden (2016) — dir. Park Chan-wook
Synopsis: 1930s Korea, in the period of Japanese occupation, a new girl, Sook-hee, is hired as a handmaiden to a Japanese heiress, Hideko, who lives a secluded life on a large countryside estate with her domineering Uncle Kouzuki. But the maid has a secret. She is a pickpocket recruited by a swindler posing as a Japanese Count to help him seduce the Lady to steal her fortune.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Adaptation of the story from Victorian Britain to 1930s colonial Korea: The Handmaiden transposes Sarah Waters's novel 'Fingersmith' from Victorian London to Korea under Japanese rule, with characters speaking both Korean and Japanese and the script colour-coding the two languages with subtitles.
- The alliance between Sook-hee (lower class) and Hideko (aristocracy): In The Handmaiden, the pickpocket Sook-hee is planted as handmaiden to the heiress Hideko to help defraud her; the two instead fall in love and turn the con against the men who arranged it.
- The erotic scenes between Sook-hee and Hideko: The Handmaiden stages two extended sex scenes between the women, the second visually echoing a pose Hideko had earlier been forced to read aloud and perform for Kouzuki's male audience.
- The film's fusion of a British novel, a colonial Korean setting, and a global art-house aesthetic: The Handmaiden combines Sarah Waters's English source, a Korea-under-Japan setting, a manor mixing English and Japanese architecture, and a polished international-festival visual style.
- The destruction of Kouzuki's pornographic book collection: In The Handmaiden, Sook-hee and Hideko tear, soak, and fling Kouzuki's antique erotic books into the basement pond, watching the pages dissolve in water.
- The film's three-part narrative structure that reveals and reframes information: 
- The hybrid architecture of Kouzuki's mansion: 
- The film's sound design, particularly the juxtaposition of reading voices, bells, and silence: In The Handmaiden, Hideko's recitations to a male audience, the manor's summoning bell, and stretches of near-silence are layered across the soundtrack, voices often heard before their speakers appear.

FILM: The Hangover (2009) — dir. Todd Phillips
Synopsis: When three friends finally come to after a raucous night of bachelor-party revelry, they find a baby in the closet and a tiger in the bathroom. But they can't seem to locate their best friend, Doug – who's supposed to be tying the knot. Launching a frantic search for Doug, the trio perseveres through a nasty hangover to try to make it to the church on time.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The character of Mr. Chow: In The Hangover, Mr. Chow is a naked Asian gangster who springs from a car trunk swinging a crowbar, speaks in a high-pitched accent, deals in casino debts, and reappears flanked by armed henchmen.
- The film's overall theme of irresponsible, consequence-free hedonism: The Hangover follows three men who black out, lose the groom, and spend a day reconstructing a night of theft, drugs, and destruction that ends with the wedding intact and everyone forgiven.
- The representation of female characters, particularly Melissa and Jade: In The Hangover, Melissa is Stu's controlling girlfriend who berates him by phone, while Jade is a stripper and escort who married Stu during the blackout and is treated kindly; neither drives the plot independently.
- The setting of Las Vegas and the events within it: The Hangover sets its blackout night in Las Vegas, moving through casino floors, a rooftop, a wedding chapel, hospital, and a trashed Caesars Palace suite, treating the city as a zone where ordinary rules suspend.
- The film's plot structure, which begins in medias res after the main events: The Hangover opens the morning after, with the groom missing and a trashed suite, then unfolds as the men reconstruct the forgotten night from clues, withholding the actual party until the closing photographs.
- The "Wolfpack" dynamic and male bonding rituals: In The Hangover, the men dub themselves a 'Wolfpack' in a rooftop toast, swear loyalty over a prick of blood, trade mutual insults, and finish the film with their friendship deepened by the shared ordeal.

FILM: The Hateful Eight (2015) — dir. Quentin Tarantino
Synopsis: Bounty hunters seek shelter from a raging blizzard and get caught up in a plot of betrayal and deception.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The continuous physical abuse of Daisy Domergue: In The Hateful Eight, Daisy Domergue, chained to John Ruth, is repeatedly elbowed, struck, splattered with blood and brains, and has soup thrown in her face across the film, often drawing laughter from other characters.
- The final alliance between Major Marquis Warren and Chris Mannix: In The Hateful Eight's finale, the Black Union veteran Warren and the white ex-Confederate Mannix, both wounded and dying, lie side by side and together hang Daisy Domergue, then read the Lincoln letter aloud.
- The poisoned coffee scene featuring projectile blood vomit: In The Hateful Eight, John Ruth and O.B. drink poisoned coffee and, mid-conversation, begin spewing arcs of bright blood from their mouths onto the floor and themselves before collapsing.
- The single-location setting of Minnie's Haberdashery: Most of The Hateful Eight unfolds inside Minnie's Haberdashery, a one-room snowbound stagecoach lodge whose door must be nailed shut against the blizzard, holding the eight characters together with no exit.
- The film's self-conscious narration and chaptered structure: The Hateful Eight divides into titled chapters, rewinds time to replay an earlier afternoon, and inserts an unseen narrator's voice-over that addresses the audience directly mid-film.

FILM: The Help (2011) — dir. Tate Taylor
Synopsis: Aibileen Clark is a middle-aged African-American maid who has spent her life raising white children and has recently lost her only son; Minny Jackson is an African-American maid who has often offended her employers despite her family's struggles with money and her desperate need for jobs; and Eugenia "Skeeter" Phelan is a young white woman who has recently moved back home after graduating college 

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Characterization of Aibileen Clark as a caregiver to white children.: In The Help, Aibileen Clark is shown raising the white Leefolt child, repeating the phrase 'You is kind, you is smart, you is important' while the child's own mother remains distant. She wears a uniform throughout and tends the home she doe
- Narrative structure centering on Skeeter Phelan as the protagonist and agent of change.: The Help opens and closes around Skeeter Phelan, a white college graduate who conceives, drives, and publishes the book of maids' stories. Her career launch and personal awakening bracket the film's events.
- Skeeter Phelan's motivation for writing the maids' stories.: In The Help, Skeeter pitches the maids' stories first as a newspaper column idea and then a book to a New York editor, partly to launch her writing career and escape her mother's pressure to marry. Her search for her own former maid, Consta
- The film's selective and sanitized depiction of the Civil Rights era.: The Help, set in 1963 Jackson, references the Medgar Evers assassination and segregation laws but keeps the central conflict domestic, resolving through a published book and personal reconciliations rather than mass struggle. Violence is mo
- Viola Davis's performance of Aibileen's restrained grief and eventual emotional breakdown.: In The Help, Viola Davis plays Aibileen Clark, a maid raising her seventeenth white child while grieving her own dead son; her composure cracks across the film, culminating in a late monologue as she walks away from the Leefolt house.
- Minny Jackson's "terrible awful" chocolate pie.: In The Help, Minny bakes a chocolate pie for Hilly Holbrook containing her own excrement, then watches Hilly eat two slices before revealing the ingredient. The episode recurs as a running joke and a bargaining chip across the narrative.
- The film's framing of the maids' testimonies through Skeeter's writing process.: In The Help, the maids' spoken accounts reach the audience mediated by Skeeter's typing, editing, and narration. Their words become chapters she arranges, with her voiceover bookending the material.
- The Oscar-winning performance of Octavia Spencer as Minny Jackson.: In The Help, Octavia Spencer plays Minny Jackson, a Black maid in 1960s Jackson, Mississippi, known for sharp comebacks, a feared fried-chicken recipe, and the 'Terrible Awful' pie she serves her former employer Hilly.

FILM: The Hidden Fortress (1958) — dir. Akira Kurosawa
Synopsis: In feudal Japan, during a bloody war between clans, two cowardly and greedy peasants, soldiers of a defeated army, stumble upon a mysterious man who guides them to a fortress hidden in the mountains.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The Hidden Gold: In The Hidden Fortress, the clan's treasure is hidden inside sticks of firewood and lashed to horses; it draws everyone's greed and is ultimately carried across the border to restore the clan.
- The Fire Festival: In The Hidden Fortress, the group is swept into a village fire festival where peasants dance and chant around a roaring bonfire, hurling firewood — possibly the gold-stuffed sticks — into the flames.
- Tadokoro the Enemy General: In The Hidden Fortress, the rival general bears a scarred face from his duel with Rokurota, is shamed by his clan, and ultimately switches sides, helping the fugitives escape at the climax.
- The Mountain Slopes: In The Hidden Fortress, the fugitives traverse steep, rocky mountains and ravines, tiny figures dwarfed against vast hillsides and the border crossing that lies beyond.
- General Rokurota Makabe: In The Hidden Fortress, Mifune plays the disguised general escorting the princess and gold, projecting gruff command, fighting a spear duel with an old rival, and bending to the princess's authority despite his own.
- The Two Peasants: In The Hidden Fortress, Tahei and Matashichi are bedraggled foot-soldiers who bicker, betray, and grovel their way across the war, each scheming to abandon the other for a share of gold.
- Princess Yuki: In The Hidden Fortress, the surviving heir poses as a mute servant girl, communicates in fierce glances and gestures, and only at the end speaks and commands openly, having learned the suffering of her people.

FILM: The Hobbit: An Unexpected Journey (2012) — dir. Peter Jackson
Synopsis: Bilbo Baggins, a hobbit enjoying his quiet life, is swept into an epic quest by Gandalf the Grey and thirteen dwarves who seek to reclaim their mountain home from Smaug, the dragon.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The One Ring: In The Hobbit, a plain gold band that rolls onto the cave floor and slips onto Bilbo's finger, turning him invisible. He pockets it without telling the dwarves, and uses it to escape and to spare Gollum.
- Smaug's stirring eye: The recurring withheld glimpses of the dragon in The Hobbit — gold shifting, a tail uncoiling, and finally a single vast eye snapping open beneath the treasure — the monster mostly kept off-screen and felt rather than shown.
- Riddles in the Dark: The cavern beneath the Misty Mountains in The Hobbit where Bilbo, separated from the company, encounters Gollum and they trade riddles for Bilbo's life, the ring lying forgotten on the stone between them.
- The flyover of the Shire: The recurring sweeping aerial and crane shots in The Hobbit that glide over Hobbiton's green hills, round doors, and tidy gardens, set to a warm pastoral theme, framing the home Bilbo leaves and longs for.
- Gandalf the Grey: The wandering wizard in The Hobbit who recruits Bilbo, guides the dwarves, and repeatedly vanishes when most needed, returning to turn the tide. He chooses the unlikely hobbit over a warrior and trusts in small, ordinary courage.
- Bilbo's handkerchief: In The Hobbit, Bilbo runs out his door realizing he forgot his pocket-handkerchief; later Bofur tears off a piece of cloth for him to use. The small domestic item marks the gap between hobbit comfort and the road.
- Thorin Oakenshield: The exiled dwarf prince in The Hobbit who leads the company to reclaim Erebor. Introduced arriving last, scarred, and skeptical of Bilbo; haunted by the loss of his kingdom and his grandfather's gold-sickness.

FILM: The Holdovers (2023) — dir. Alexander Payne
Synopsis: A curmudgeonly instructor at a New England prep school is forced to remain on campus during Christmas break to babysit the handful of students with nowhere to go. Eventually, he forms an unlikely bond with one of them — a damaged, brainy troublemaker — and with the school’s head cook, who has just lost a son in Vietnam.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Mary Lamb in the empty kitchen: In The Holdovers, head cook Mary Lamb stays on campus over break, grieving her son Curtis, killed in Vietnam after the school he attended on scholarship couldn't keep him out of the draft like its wealthy boys.
- Angus Tully's dislocated shoulder: In The Holdovers, troubled student Angus dislocates his shoulder on the gym floor and confides to Hunham that the same arm pops out repeatedly — a recurring injury he hides, like the family secret he carries about his institutionalized fath
- The period film grain and 1970s look: The Holdovers is shot to resemble a movie actually made around 1971 — soft film grain, faded color, vintage studio logos, scratchy optical dissolves, a dated zoom, and freeze-frames that mimic the New Hollywood era.
- Barton Academy over Christmas break: In The Holdovers, the New England prep school empties for the holidays, leaving snowbound stone buildings, dark dormitories, a frozen campus and a single boiler running for the handful left behind.
- Paul Hunham's wandering eye and fish odor: In The Holdovers, the classics master Hunham is built from afflictions: a lazy eye that won't meet anyone straight, a medical condition that makes him smell of fish, and a tongue that hurls Latin insults to keep students at arm's length.
- The borrowed Christmas dinner and the bar trio: Throughout The Holdovers, the three strangers cobble together substitute family rituals — a makeshift Christmas dinner, a tree, a New Year's drink, a Boston outing — sharing meals and confessions none of them have anyone else to share with.
- Hunham's final lie to save Angus: At the end of The Holdovers, Hunham takes the blame for Angus's unauthorized visit to his father, confessing to invented misconduct so the boy won't be expelled — and is fired for it, leaving Barton for good.

FILM: The Host (2006) — dir. Bong Joon Ho
Synopsis: A teenage girl is captured by a giant mutated squid-like creature that appears from Seoul's Han River after toxic waste was dumped in it, prompting her family into a frantic search for her.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Park Gang-du: In The Host, the dozing, peroxide-haired snack-stand attendant and single father, prone to falling asleep on the job, who drops the wrong hand in the panic and loses his daughter to the creature.
- The Sewer Lair: In The Host, the creature's nest is a vast circular drainage tunnel beneath the city, its lower pit littered with human bones, where it deposits living captives including Hyun-seo.
- The Creature: In The Host, a bus-sized amphibious mutant emerges from the Han River in broad daylight, swinging from bridge struts and snatching crowds with a prehensile tail. It is fully shown early rather than hidden.
- The Family Photo on the Altar: In The Host, the grieving family collapses together on the gymnasium floor in a writhing knot of weeping bodies, and later sets Hyun-seo's portrait among funeral offerings — the household drawn as a single sprawling organism.
- The Phantom Virus: In The Host, authorities announce the monster carries a deadly virus, quarantining and gassing the city, though no virus is ever confirmed and the diagnosis appears fabricated.
- Park Nam-joo's Bow: In The Host, the aunt is a competitive archer whose habitual fatal flaw is hesitating too long before releasing; her bow and final arrow become the family's weapon against the creature in the climax.
- Tonal Whiplash: In The Host, scenes lurch between broad slapstick, raw grief, satirical news footage, and brutal horror — the gym mourning collapses into farce, a death scene plays beside comedy, registers colliding within single sequences.

FILM: The House That Jack Built (2018) — dir. Lars von Trier
Synopsis: Failed architect, engineer and vicious murderer Jack narrates the details of some of his most elaborately orchestrated crimes, each of them a towering piece of art that defines his life's work as a serial killer for twelve years.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The murder of "Simple" (Jacqueline).: In The House That Jack Built, Jack mutilates a woman he nicknames 'Simple,' cutting off her breasts in a prolonged sequence. Earlier he had paraded her through a city street screaming for help while passersby ignore her.
- Jack's OCD and his repeated returns to the crime scene.: In The House That Jack Built, Jack, an obsessive-compulsive, drives back to a victim's house convinced he left a blood spot, scrubbing and rechecking the floor under heavy rain until water erases the evidence.
- Matt Dillon's performance as Jack.: In The House That Jack Built, Matt Dillon plays Jack across deadpan calm, stiff feigned smiles, sudden flares of rage, and direct philosophical narration, often addressing the unseen Verge in even, lecturing tones.
- The film's controversial premiere and media reception.: The House That Jack Built premiered at Cannes 2018 amid reported walkouts and outrage, with press coverage foregrounding audience exits and von Trier's earlier festival ban, the scandal preceding most viewers' actual encounter with the film
- The final scene of Jack falling into the abyss.: In The House That Jack Built, the closing sequence follows Jack and Verge through a glowing infernal landscape. Jack attempts to climb a crumbling rock bridge over a pit, loses his grip, and plummets into the void as the credits begin over 
- The repeated use of David Bowie's song "Fame".: In The House That Jack Built, David Bowie's 'Fame' recurs across the film, including over montages of Jack's life and crimes and over the closing fall into the abyss, its bright funk groove playing against the grim imagery.
- The final house constructed from victims' bodies.: In The House That Jack Built, after failing to build a real house, Jack assembles a dwelling from frozen corpses stacked in a freezer, then enters and exits it through the doorway before his descent into the underworld.
- Jack's digressions on art, Glenn Gould, and Nazi architecture.: In The House That Jack Built, Jack interrupts his confessions with illustrated lectures on Glenn Gould, Gothic cathedrals, Albert Speer's ruin-value architecture, and decaying grapes, splicing archival footage and stills into the murder nar
- The dialogue and relationship between Jack and Verge.: In The House That Jack Built, Jack's voiceover confession is answered throughout by Verge, an unseen older voice who interrupts, scolds, and finally guides Jack on a descent through a literal underworld toward a chasm.
- The first "incident" with the Woman on the roadside.: In The House That Jack Built, the first murder begins when a stranded woman with a broken car jack flags Jack down. She is talkative and abrasive, repeatedly suggesting he could be a killer, before he eventually bludgeons her with the jack

FILM: The Housemaid (1960) — dir. Kim Ki-young
Synopsis: A piano composer's family moves into a new house; when his pregnant wife collapses from working to support the family, he hires a housemaid to help with housework.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The two-storey house: In The Housemaid, the family's newly built Western-style home with its central staircase contains nearly all the action; the maid sleeps below, the family lives above, and the stairs become the route of every transgression.
- The housemaid: Lee Eun-shim's maid in The Housemaid arrives as cheap help, becomes the composer's lover, and then weaponizes her pregnancy and knowledge of the affair to seize power over the household.
- Rat poison: In The Housemaid a box of rat poison sits in the home and recurs as the household's casual instrument of death, used and threatened against children and adults as the family unravels.
- The closing direct address: The Housemaid frames its grim story with a domestic scene and ends by having the composer turn and speak to the camera, addressing the audience directly with a knowing warning about the tale.
- The pregnant wife: In The Housemaid the wife sews piecework late into the night to fund the new house, collapses from exhaustion while pregnant, and her breakdown is the reason the maid is hired in the first place.
- Windows and glass walls: The Housemaid repeatedly frames characters through and behind the home's large windows and glass partitions, watching one another between rooms, in the rain, across the divide of floor and class.
- The piano: The composer in The Housemaid teaches piano and composes at the upright instrument upstairs; music lessons bring young women into the home and the piano room becomes a charged site of attraction and labor.

messages.content:
FILM: The Howling (1981) — dir. Joe Dante
Synopsis: After a bizarre and near fatal encounter with a serial killer, a newswoman is sent to a rehabilitation center whose inhabitants may not be what they seem.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The TV set as constant presence: In The Howling, television screens are everywhere — Karen's newscast, monitors in the studio, the diner set at the finale — and cartoons, ads, and news bleed through scenes as ambient texture.
- Eddie Quist's transformation in the office: In The Howling, the killer Eddie Quist, cornered by Karen, undergoes a slow, agonizing werewolf transformation in full light — bones cracking, skin bubbling, snout extending — rendered entirely through practical effects.
- Karen's on-air transformation: In The Howling, newswoman Karen White's trauma plays out twice as televised spectacle — first her near-murder, finally her live, broadcast partial werewolf change as proof for an audience that won't believe her words.
- Dr. George Waggner: In The Howling, Dr. George Waggner is the soft-spoken therapist running the Colony, a writer-philosopher who believes the werewolf nature can be controlled and integrated rather than denied, and who ultimately fails to hold his community to
- Pino Donaggio's lush score: In The Howling, Pino Donaggio's orchestral score swells with romantic and melodramatic warmth, often playing earnest emotional cues against scenes of stalking, dread, and grotesque transformation.
- The Colony retreat: In The Howling, the wooded therapy resort run by Dr. Waggner houses a community of patients who turn out to be werewolves, blending group encounter sessions with predatory ritual under the trees.
- The character names as monster-movie tribute: In The Howling, characters and businesses are named after directors of earlier werewolf and horror films — Waggner, Quist, and others — seeding the film with insider nods to genre history.

FILM: The Hudsucker Proxy (1994) — dir. Joel Coen
Synopsis: A naive business graduate is installed as president of a manufacturing company as part of a stock scam.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Norville Barnes: In The Hudsucker Proxy, Tim Robbins plays the wide-eyed business-school graduate from Muncie who is installed as president to be a fool, clutching his rolled-up hula-hoop drawing through every meeting.
- The Art-Deco corporate skyscraper: In The Hudsucker Proxy the Hudsucker Industries tower is a towering, stylized Deco monolith of marble lobbies, executive penthouses up top and a windowless mailroom in the bowels, shot in cavernous wide angles.
- Sidney J. Mussburger: In The Hudsucker Proxy, Paul Newman plays the chain-smoking board chairman who engineers the scam — installing an idiot president to crater the stock so insiders can buy cheap before the founder's shares hit the public.
- Amy Archer's machine-gun patter: In The Hudsucker Proxy, Jennifer Jason Leigh plays a Pulitzer-hungry reporter who goes undercover; her dialogue is delivered in a clipped, rapid-fire 1940s newspaper-picture cadence, often overlapping and breathless.
- The falling man on New Year's Eve: In The Hudsucker Proxy the film opens and circles back to a body plummeting from the skyscraper toward the street as the year turns — first the founder Waring Hudsucker, then Norville, the descent shot from above and below repeatedly.
- The Hula Hoop: In The Hudsucker Proxy, Norville Barnes's wordless circle of plastic — pitched on a single blank page reading only a drawn circle — collapses unsold, then sweeps the nation when one boy spins it in the street.
- The Hudsucker Building clock: In The Hudsucker Proxy a vast Art-Deco clock crowns the company tower; its hands are stopped and restarted by hand by the janitor Moses, who narrates from inside the gearworks.

FILM: The Hunger Games (2012) — dir. Gary Ross
Synopsis: In a dystopian society where the Capitol forces each district to send two young tributes to fight to the death in a televised spectacle, a girl volunteers to take her sister’s place, setting the stage for a struggle of survival and defiance.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Katniss's pre-Games interview dress reveal: In The Hunger Games, Katniss spins on stage during her televised interview and her gown ignites into a swirl of synthetic flame as the Capitol crowd gasps and cheers.
- The character of Rue and her relationship with Katniss: In The Hunger Games, Rue is the small tribute from District 11 who allies with Katniss; after Rue is speared, Katniss sings to her, covers her body in flowers, and raises three fingers, prompting a riot in District 11.
- The Gamemakers' control room: In The Hunger Games, Seneca Crane and his technicians stand in a dark, glowing chamber manipulating a holographic arena, conjuring fireballs and mutant hounds and altering rules with hand gestures on touch-screens.
- The integrated 'on-screen' graphics showing Tribute deaths and audience reactions: Throughout The Hunger Games, the arena action is overlaid with broadcast graphics, the cannon-and-portrait death announcements, and intercut shots of Capitol audiences and District crowds watching on screens.
- The Reaping ceremony in District 12: In The Hunger Games, District 12 children are herded into roped pens, scanned by blood-prick, and watched over by peacekeepers while Effie draws names from glass bowls; Katniss volunteers in her sister's place.
- Peeta's declaration of love for Katniss during his pre-Games interview: During The Hunger Games interview segment, Peeta tells Caesar Flickerman that a girl he has loved came with him to the Capitol, then admits she doesn't know, as the crowd swoons and Katniss reacts with anger backstage.
- The use of shaky, handheld camera work during the Cornucopia bloodbath: In The Hunger Games, the opening arena slaughter at the Cornucopia is shot with rapid handheld camera movement, fragmented cutting, and partial framings that withhold clear views of the killings.

FILM: The Hunt (2012) — dir. Thomas Vinterberg
Synopsis: A teacher lives a lonely life, all the while struggling over his son’s custody. His life slowly gets better as he finds love and receives good news from his son, but his new luck is about to be brutally shattered by an innocent little lie.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):

- The community's collective shunning of Lucas (e.g., supermarket scene, son's dog being killed).: In The Hunt, the townspeople refuse Lucas service and beat him in the supermarket, bar him from shops, and someone kills his son's dog and leaves it for the family to find.
- The final scene where an unseen figure shoots at Lucas in the woods.: In The Hunt's closing scene, a year later, Lucas hunts in the forest; a rifle shot rings out and a backlit, unseen figure stands among the trees before walking off, leaving Lucas unharmed but shaken.
- The psychologist's interview with Klara.: In The Hunt, a man brought in to question Klara sits with her in a soft room, asking leading questions and offering reassurance until the child's vague nods and silences are recorded as confirmation of abuse.
- The character of Klara and her initial lie.: In The Hunt, Klara, a small girl who adores Lucas, tells the kindergarten head a vague, upsetting thing about him after he gently rebuffs her crush; she later tries to retract it, saying she said something foolish.
- The film's cinematography, particularly the use of handheld cameras and natural lighting.: The Hunt is shot largely with handheld cameras and available light, favouring shallow autumnal palettes, close framing on faces, and an unsteady, observational closeness to its actors.
- The rapid spread of the rumor throughout the town's social network.: In The Hunt, an offhand remark by a child reaches the kindergarten head, then parents, then the wider town. FILM: The Hunt for Red October (1990) — dir. John McTiernan
Synopsis: A new technologically-superior Soviet nuclear sub, the Red October, is heading for the U.S. coast under the command of Captain Marko Ramius. The American government thinks Ramius is planning to attack. Lone CIA analyst Jack Ryan has a different idea: he thinks Ramius is planning to defect, but he has only a few hours to find him and prove it - because the entire Russian naval and air commands are 

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Cinematography and sound design of submarine interiors and sonar sequences: In The Hunt for Red October, submarine interiors are lit in cold blues and red battle-lighting, with tight framing in cramped corridors. Sonar sequences isolate single technicians wearing headphones, the soundtrack reduced to amplified ping
- The screenplay's relationship to Tom Clancy's source novel: The Hunt for Red October adapts Tom Clancy's dense technical novel, compressing its detailed procedural chapters and multiple plot threads into a roughly two-hour film centered on Ryan and Ramius.

FILM: The Hurt Locker (2008) — dir. Kathryn Bigelow
Synopsis: During the Iraq War, a Sergeant recently assigned to an army bomb squad is put at odds with his squad mates due to his maverick way of handling his work.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Sergeant William James: The maverick EOD technician of The Hurt Locker who counts his disarmed bombs by the hundreds, ignores protocol, and grows visibly restless away from the wire.
- The countdown intertitle: The Hurt Locker periodically stamps the screen with a number — 'Days Left in Rotation: 38' — counting down to the team's end-of-tour, the only formal nod to a finish line.
- The cellphone detonator: In The Hurt Locker, the recurring sight of a civilian holding a mobile phone near a bomb site — the everyday object that might, or might not, be the trigger for a remote charge.
- Sergeant Sanborn: James's by-the-book teammate in The Hurt Locker, who tracks protocol, openly resents James's recklessness, and late in the film confesses he is done and wants a son.
- The bomb suit: In The Hurt Locker, the heavy padded EOD suit James dons to walk toward live ordnance — bulky, helmeted, slow, leaving him isolated on the long approach.
- Handheld, multi-camera framing: The Hurt Locker's restless documentary-style shooting: jittery zooms, multiple cameras catching the same disarmament from scattered angles, sudden snaps to rooftops and onlookers.
- The boy 'Beckham': A young Iraqi street vendor who sells DVDs and banters with James in The Hurt Locker; James later believes the boy's body has been used as a 'body bomb,' and the certainty unravels.

FILM: The Idiots (1998) — dir. Lars von Trier
Synopsis: A group of people gather at a Copenhagen suburban home to break all the limitations and to bring out the 'inner idiot' in themselves.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The handheld, intruding camera: Per Dogme rules, The Idiots is shot on handheld digital video — jittery, zooming, occasionally letting a boom or crew member slip into frame. The image is grainy, available-light, restless.
- Stoffer: The charismatic ringleader of The Idiots, who founded the experiment and enforces its purity. He goads, manipulates, and stages tests; in one scene he runs naked and screaming through the suburb when challenged.
- The group orgy: In one notorious sequence of The Idiots, the 'spassing' dissolves into a real, partly unsimulated group sex scene among the housemates, filmed with the same handheld looseness as everything else.
- The off-screen director's voice: At several points in The Idiots, von Trier's own voice is audible off-camera, questioning the characters during the documentary interviews — folding the maker into the fiction as an interrogating presence.
- The act of 'spassing': In The Idiots, members of the group slacken their faces, drool, and grunt in public — performing disability to provoke and to liberate. The film calls this 'spassing,' staged in restaurants, factories, swimming pools.
- The suburban villa: The Idiots unfolds almost entirely inside a large empty house in suburban Søllerød that the group occupies — owned by an absent uncle, slated for sale. It functions as clubhouse, dormitory, and stage.
- Karen: The grieving outsider of The Idiots, drawn into the commune almost by accident. Quiet, watchful, she barely participates — until the final scene, where she alone passes the group's ultimate test among her own family.

messages.content:
FILM: The Imitation Game (2014) — dir. Morten Tyldum
Synopsis: Based on the real life story of legendary cryptanalyst Alan Turing, the film portrays the nail-biting race against time by Turing and his brilliant team of code-breakers at Britain's top-secret Government Code and Cypher School at Bletchley Park, during the darkest days of World War II.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Alan Turing: The cryptanalyst protagonist of The Imitation Game: brilliant, literal-minded, socially abrasive, hiding both his methods and his homosexuality, played across three timelines from school to wartime to post-war prosecution.
- The cyanide-laced apple: The half-eaten apple referenced in The Imitation Game's closing material, tied to Turing's death by cyanide poisoning after his chemical castration — the film's final, quiet image of a man undone.
- Christopher, the bombe machine: In The Imitation Game, the rotating drum-and-wire decryption machine Turing builds and names after his dead schoolboy love, churning relentlessly through Enigma settings as the team waits.
- Joan Clarke: The crossword-puzzle prodigy in The Imitation Game who joins Turing's team despite being a woman, becomes his fiancée of convenience, and refuses to abandon him.
- The Bletchley Park huts: The drab wooden huts and grand manor of Bletchley Park in The Imitation Game, where the code-breakers work in absolute secrecy, forbidden to discuss their tasks even with each other.
- The Enigma cipher: The German encryption recurring throughout The Imitation Game as the impossible problem — the daily-resetting code with millions of millions of settings that the team must crack before midnight each day.
- The three-timeline cross-cut: The Imitation Game's editing structure, weaving Turing's 1951 police interrogation, his wartime Bletchley years, and his 1920s schooldays, letting one era comment on another through juxtaposition.

Produce the Cinematic Invitation AND the bold takes now (takes: 0–3 per framework across all 14, potent only, intent-independent, each with theorist/concept/real_person metadata).

FILM: The Imposter (2012) — dir. Bart Layton
Synopsis: In 1994, a 13-year-old boy disappeared without a trace from his home in San Antonio, Texas. Three-and-a-half years later, he is found alive in a village in southern Spain with a horrifying story of kidnap and torture. His family is overjoyed to bring him home. But all is not quite as it seems.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Frédéric Bourdin's direct testimony: In The Imposter, the con man narrates his own deception straight to camera, smiling, coaching the viewer through each lie as it lands.
- The family's belief: In The Imposter, the missing boy's mother and sister embrace a brown-eyed adult stranger as their blue-eyed teenage Nicholas, accepting his accent and altered appearance.
- San Antonio, Texas: The Imposter roots itself in a working-class San Antonio household — modest interiors, the boy's bedroom, the freeways and strip-lit streets where he vanished and to which the stranger returns.
- The reenactment footage: The Imposter dramatizes its events with actors and slick staging — airports, phone booths, dim interiors — cut seamlessly against the real interview subjects.
- Charlie Parker, the private investigator: In The Imposter, a folksy Texan private eye recounts how he cracked the case by studying the ears and eyes in a single photograph, then chases a darker theory of his own.
- The tape recorder and phone calls: The Imposter dwells on the long-distance phone calls and recordings through which Bourdin first reaches the family across an ocean, coaching himself into Nicholas's voice.
- The blue eyes / brown eyes: The Imposter returns repeatedly to the physical mismatch — Nicholas Barclay's blue eyes versus Bourdin's brown — held up as the obvious tell everyone ignored.

FILM: The Innocents (2021) — dir. Eskil Vogt
Synopsis: Four children become friends during the summer holidays, and out of sight of the adults they discover they have hidden powers. While exploring their newfound abilities in the nearby forests and playgrounds, their innocent play takes a dark turn and strange things begin to happen.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Ben: In The Innocents, the small boy who can move objects with his mind and feels no flinch when he kills; he tests his power on a cat before turning it on people.
- The silent telepathic link: Throughout The Innocents, children communicate mind-to-mind across distances; conversations happen in stillness, faces holding while voices arrive without lips moving.
- The cat: Early in The Innocents, a stray cat becomes the children's first test subject — tormented, then dropped down a stairwell by Ben while the others watch.
- Anna: In The Innocents, Ida's severely autistic, nonverbal older sister, who through Aisha's telepathy gains a voice and inner life her family never knew.
- Aisha: In The Innocents, the gentle girl with vitiligo who can hear thoughts and feel others' pain; she becomes the moral counterweight to Ben.
- The sound design of small impacts: In The Innocents, the score recedes and dread is built from amplified everyday sounds — a cat's body hitting concrete, glass cracking, a bottlecap twisted by an unseen force.
- The housing estate and its playground: The Innocents unfolds almost entirely around identical concrete apartment blocks, a sandbox, a thin forest edge and stairwells — a Norwegian suburb emptied by summer holiday.

FILM: The Insect Woman (1963) — dir. Shohei Imamura
Synopsis: A woman, Tome, is born to a lower class family in Japan in 1918. The title refers to an insect, repeating its mistakes, as in an infinite circle. Imamura, with this metaphor, introduces the life of Tome, who keeps trying to change her poor life.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The breastfeeding and incest undertones: The Insect Woman foregrounds bodily appetite — Tome's father suckling at her breast as an infant, charged physical intimacy between family members, and recurring images of eating, nursing, and coupling.
- The brothel and boarding-house: In The Insect Woman, much of Tome's adult life unfolds in cramped urban rooms — brothels and lodging houses where women work, sleep, scheme, and are bought and sold within thin walls.
- The repeated mountain-climb: In The Insect Woman, Imamura intercuts a recurring image of a small figure trudging up a steep snow-covered slope, returning at structural turning points in Tome's life.
- Tome: In The Insect Woman, Tome is born in 1918 to a poor rural family and survives through factory work, prostitution, brothel-keeping, and betrayal. Sachiko Hidari plays her aging from girlhood to weathered middle age.
- The freeze-frame and dated intertitle: The Insect Woman halts the action into still frames stamped with dates and proverbs, interrupting scenes to mark the passage of years and comment on events.
- The daughter Nobuko: In The Insect Woman, Tome's daughter grows up to reject her mother's world, taking a lover and a small farm rather than repeating the cycle of urban exploitation.
- The rural family compound: The Insect Woman opens and returns to a poor northern farming household — earthen floors, animals, communal sleeping, and the rhythm of seasonal labor binding the family to the land.

FILM: The Insult (2017) — dir. Ziad Doueiri
Synopsis: After an emotional exchange between a Lebanese Christian and a Palestinian refugee escalates, the men end up in a court case that gets national attention.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The drainpipe: In The Insult a small illegally rigged gutter on Toni's balcony splashes water onto Yasser below; his unauthorized repair, smashed by Toni, ignites the entire conflict.
- Toni Hanna: The Lebanese Christian garage owner in The Insult who demands an apology, listens to Phalangist speeches, and slowly reveals a childhood survivor's wound beneath his belligerence.
- Yasser Salameh: The Palestinian refugee construction foreman in The Insult, skilled, restrained, and provoked into a single punch that detonates the legal storm; he later quietly goads Toni into striking back.
- The courtroom and its broadcast: In The Insult the trial moves from a small court to a televised national spectacle, with crowds, riot police, and live news cameras outside transforming a private quarrel into political theater.
- The Phalangist speech recording: In The Insult Toni repeatedly listens to recorded Bachir Gemayel oratory in his garage, the audio playing as he works, anchoring his sense of grievance and identity.
- The reconciling handshake of fathers: Across The Insult, the two opposing lawyers turn out to be estranged father and daughter, and the film repeatedly stages near-reconciliations through small private gestures between adversaries.
- The contested word: In The Insult an actual insult — Toni's wished-for erasure of Yasser's people — becomes the legal and emotional fulcrum, debated, quoted, and reinterpreted by everyone in court and on the street.

FILM: The Intouchables (2011) — dir. Éric Toledano
Synopsis: A true story of two men who should never have met – a quadriplegic aristocrat who was injured in a paragliding accident and a young man from the projects.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- Driss loudly laughing during the opera performance: In The Intouchables, Driss sits in a private opera box beside Philippe and bursts into loud laughter at the costumed singer, while surrounding patrons stay silent and composed.
- Driss's intervention in Philippe's epistolary relationship with Éléonore: In The Intouchables, Driss reads Philippe's letters to his pen pal Éléonore, mocks their formality, urges a phone call, and eventually engineers a real meeting between the two.
- Philippe's quadriplegia: In The Intouchables, Philippe is a wealthy man paralysed from the neck down after a paragliding accident, dependent on caregivers for every physical need and unable to feel sensation below the neck.
- The contrast between Philippe's mansion and Driss's housing project: In The Intouchables, the film cuts between Philippe's gilded Paris townhouse with sweeping staircases and Driss's crowded family flat in a high-rise estate on the city's edge.
- The end credits sequence showing footage of the real Philippe and Abdel: The Intouchables ends with documentary footage of the real Philippe Pozzo di Borgo and Abdel Sellou, shown over the closing credits, following the film's 'based on a true story' framing.
- The paragliding scene: In The Intouchables, Driss arranges for the quadriplegic Philippe to go paragliding in the mountains; the two fly tandem above the landscape, and Philippe, who was injured in a paragliding accident, returns to the sky.
- The shaving scene where Driss cares for Philippe: In The Intouchables, Driss shaves Philippe's face, at one point sculpting and trimming his beard and moustache into comic shapes before they settle into an ordinary clean shave, the two laughing together.
- Driss's character arc: In The Intouchables, Driss enters as a hard-up applicant collecting a rejection signature for benefits and exits having reawakened Philippe's appetite for living, before returning to job-seeking and family duty.
- The close-ups of Driss's hands caring for Philippe's body (e.g., putting on compression stockings): In The Intouchables, the camera moves in close as Driss's hands roll compression stockings onto Philippe's legs, wash, dress and reposition a body that cannot feel the contact.
- The job interview sequence from Philippe's point of view: In The Intouchables, candidates for the caregiver job are filmed across a desk as Philippe, unseen behind his assistant, watches and assesses them. Driss enters not to be hired but to get a signature for benefits.
- The juxtaposition of Vivaldi's "The Four Seasons" and Earth, Wind & Fire's "Boogie Wonderland": In The Intouchables, Philippe quizzes Driss on classical pieces, including Vivaldi; later Driss commandeers the stereo at Philippe's birthday and replaces the orchestra with Earth, Wind & Fire's 'Boogie Wonderland,' getting the formally dre
- The scene where Driss replaces Philippe's high-end leg cream with a common foot cream.: In The Intouchables, Driss swaps Philippe's expensive specialist leg cream for an ordinary cheap foot cream, one of several practical jokes he plays during his caregiving.

FILM: The Invisible Man (2020) — dir. Leigh Whannell
Synopsis: When Cecilia's abusive ex takes his own life and leaves her his fortune, she suspects his death was a hoax. As a series of coincidences turn lethal, Cecilia works to prove that she is being hunted by someone nobody can see.

FIGURES (anchor each take to one of these by exact label):
- The Empty Corner of the Frame: Throughout The Invisible Man, the camera holds on rooms where nothing visibly happens — panning slowly to empty doorways, hallways, and the air beside Cecilia. Compositions leave unmotivated negative space.
- Sourceless Footsteps and Breath: The Invisible Man builds tension from sound with no body — a creaking floorboard, a held breath, a chair shifting in an empty kitchen. The score drops out to let nothing be heard loudly.
- Cecilia Kass: In The Invisible Man, Cecilia is a woman who flees a controlling architect-husband, then is hunted by a presence no one else can detect. Elisabeth Moss plays her flinching, watchful, gradually weaponized.
- The Restaurant Throat-Slit: In The Invisible Man, a pivotal public attack has Cecilia's sister killed with a kitchen knife pressed into Cecilia's own hand — the violence committed by an unseen force but framed as if she did it.
- Adrian's Glass House: In The Invisible Man, Adrian's clifftop home is a fortress of glass walls, security cameras, and minimalist concrete — a transparent box that paradoxically lets nothing out and watches everything within.
- Adrian Griffin: In The Invisible Man, Adrian is the wealthy optics inventor and abuser who fakes his suicide, becomes invisible to hunt Cecilia, and frames his brother — played as charming, controlled, and emotionally flat.
- The Invisibility Suit: In The Invisible Man, the threat is not magic but a wearable rig of micro-cameras covering the body, bending light. It is revealed as a black bodysuit studded with lenses, hung on a mannequin.
